Entertainment.title: Sex, drugs and amoebic dysentery: the 20 best making-of documentaries – ranked!
Entertainment.text:
20. Document of the Dead (1985)

Behind-the-scenes footage from Dawn of the Dead is the highlight of this aficionados-only affair, which follows the 1979 satirical zombie horror all the way through to distribution. Director George A Romero, makeup maestro Tom Savini and the occasional zombie actor shoot the breeze in the deserted shopping mall that provides the movie with its incongruous central location.

19. The Death of “Superman Lives”: What Happened? (2015)

Imagining what might have been if Tim Burton’s Superman Lives had got off the ground, documentary maker Jon Schnepp cosies up on screen with his interviewees and insinuates himself unforgivably into the story. The material is almost good enough to transcend his vanity: there is test footage of lead actor Nicolas Cage in his Man of Steel duds, plus interviews with Burton, original screenwriter Kevin Smith and producer Jon Peters, who was adamant that Superman should fight polar bears and a giant spider.

18. Becoming Bulletproof (2014)

A group of actors with disabilities form the bulk of the cast of the short western Bulletproof, shot in the California desert courtesy of the inclusive arts project Zeno Mountain Farm. Crucially, Bulletproof itself isn’t about disability, but rather an attempt to highlight the lack of on-screen representation – and plug the gap. This affectionate documentary tracks the film from preproduction to premiere.

17. They’ll Love Me When I’m Dead (2018)

Orson Welles spent five years shooting what became his final film, The Other Side of the Wind, with three years elapsing before its star – director and sometime actor John Huston – even stepped in front of the camera. After all that, the footage ended up impounded by the Iranian revolutionary government. A version eventually premiered in 2018 and is now on Netflix, along with this scattershot documentary, presented by Alan Cumming, which strings together archive footage, new interviews and typically Wellesian stories of on-set bluffs, tomfoolery and procrastination.

16. Filmmaker: A Diary by George Lucas (1968)

A half-hour snapshot by Lucas of his new buddy Francis Ford Coppola, who is hard at work on his fourth film, The Rain People, and not too shy to argue with his lead actor, Shirley Knight. Contains one choice detail: in preparation for driving across the country shooting this road movie, all the men on the crew, Coppola included, shave off their beards to look more presentable for any hippy-hating officials they might encounter along the way.

15. Boorman and the Devil (2025)

In declining The Exorcist but taking on Exorcist II: The Heretic, John Boorman perhaps displayed a preference for poisoned chalices over champagne flutes. He is candid and good-humoured, if still a little shell-shocked, as he recounts the experience of filming the sequel once derided as “the stupidest major movie ever made”, and the despair that led him to contemplate self-immolation on Hollywood Boulevard. Sand-related illness, a sozzled Richard Burton, locusts and tap-dancing: this has it all.

14. Doomed! The Untold Story of Roger Corman’s The Fantastic Four (2015)

Filmed in a rat-infested studio on sets recycled from the Jurassic Park rip-off Carnosaur, with special effects entrusted to a local outfit called Mr Film, this cheapo superhero adventure was made in a rush to prevent the rights to The Fantastic Four reverting from producer Bernd Eichinger to Marvel. (“That movie was never supposed to be shown to anybody,” said Stan Lee.) This heartening documentary, which shows the crestfallen cast refusing to let their film die, feels even more pertinent after Warner Bros recently shelved some movies as tax write-offs, including Batgirl and Coyote Vs Acme, the latter rescued only by the skin of its teeth.

13. Jodorowsky’s Dune (2013)

In trying to adapt Frank Herbert’s Dune in the mid-1970s, cinematic shaman Alejandro Jodorowsky (Santa Sangre, El Topo) bit off more than he could chew, just as David Lynch would when his version came to painful fruition in 1984. But Frank Pavich’s documentary proves that Jodorowsky’s intention to make “a film that gives LSD hallucinations without taking LSD” was not too fanciful. Among those in his corner were the artist HR Giger, who went on to design the monsters in Alien, and a cast including Salvador Dalí, Mick Jagger and Orson Welles, with the latter being bribed to take part with the promise of having his favourite chef on set.

12. Lost Soul: The Doomed Journey of Richard Stanley’s Island of Dr Moreau (2014)

When the studio New Line tried to ditch South African director Richard Stanley from his own HG Wells adaptation, he asked a warlock called Skip to pull some cosmic strings. That did the trick for a while, helping Stanley to charm the film’s star, Marlon Brando. But black magic was no match for cast member Val Kilmer, who demanded a 40% reduction in his own shooting days, then spent his time on set playing power games. There was nature to contend with, too, in the form of wild animals (a puma pisses on Stanley’s tailored suit) and a hurricane that ravages the location in Cairns, Queensland. Finally replaced by curmudgeonly veteran John Frankenheimer, Stanley refuses to leave Australia, which is when things go from mad to worse.

11. No Frank in Lumberton (1988) / Blue Velvet Revisited (2016)

Two behind-the-scenes Blue Velvet documentaries from one director. Peter Braatz was still a film student when David Lynch, with whom he had been corresponding for several years, invited him to Wilmington, North Carolina in 1985 to chart the making of what would become his twisted masterpiece. Braatz marshalled just under an hour of the resulting Super-8 material into his 1988 documentary, which straddled the line between orthodox and experimental. He then reshaped it into a full-on ambient head-trip for the 86-minute 2016 version, which mixes flickering footage and crisp black-and-white photographs with a woozy score and the voices of Lynch, Dennis Hopper and others to form an ethereal audiovisual collage.

10. The Sweatbox (2002)

Disney had high hopes for Kingdom of the Sun, a Prince and the Pauper-style animated musical drama set in the Inca empire. The studio sent Lion King co-director Roger Allers on a research trip to Peru and commissioned a suite of new songs by Sting. But it was back to the drawing board after a calamitous screening of an early rough cut; Allers and Sting were given the heave-ho, and the movie was retooled as the larky comedy The Emperor’s New Groove. Sting’s wife, Trudie Styler, charts every disastrous step in a documentary that Disney has done its darnedest to suppress.

9. From Darkness to Light (2024)

A 10-a-penny title for an account of a once-in-a-lifetime film-making folly: Jerry Lewis’s abandoned, incomplete 1972 Holocaust drama The Day The Clown Cried. Directing himself as a former clown who entertains children in a concentration camp, Lewis made a misguided bid to be taken seriously. “It was bad work,” he admits here. It wasn’t only the dubious material that defeated the former Nutty Professor: unbeknown to him, the option on the script had expired, rendering the entire project illegal. It was his decision, though, to hire a repentant former concentration camp guard as part of the crew. “He was a human being!” Lewis protests.

8. Poultry in Motion: Truth Is Stranger Than Chicken (2008)

Seventy-odd fans of horror exploitation studio Troma worked unpaid on Poultrygeist: Night of the Chicken Dead while living in a deserted church in a rundown corner of Buffalo, New York, with one cold shower between them. Meanwhile, the chicken-themed zombie flick was shot at a nearby abandoned McDonald’s. This documentary captures all the on-set horror, from the sexually disinhibited auditions to the hourly cast-and-crew bust-ups. Actors walk off, burst into tears and throw punches; a zombie extra accidentally sets himself on fire; and bilious co-director and Troma boss Lloyd Kaufman proves both lackadaisical and tyrannical.

7. Shirkers (2018)

When budding film-maker Sandi Tan met the enigmatic Georges Cardona, he cited Fitzcarraldo as his inspiration and claimed to know crew members from Apocalypse Now. Those pictures – famously troubled productions that spawned their own jaw-dropping documentaries – look like red flags considering what came next: Cardona directed Tan’s indie road movie Shirkers, swallowing up $10,000 of her savings when he ran out of money, then vanished with the resulting 70 reels of unprocessed film. She didn’t see the footage until decades later, when those reels were returned to her by Cardona’s widow. Tan’s sobering 2018 documentary attempts to make sense of the betrayal.

6. The Peddler (2010)

“Good film directors will notice many mistakes,” says prolific camcorder auteur and 67-year-old Santa Claus lookalike Daniel Burmeister. “But I like what I do: making hand-crafted films.” In exchange for a month’s food and accommodation, Burmeister sets up shop in a remote Argentinian village to bring the community together by shooting a movie from one of his own scripts. His budget may be nonexistent but his resourcefulness is boundless: in place of a dolly shot, for instance, he sits on a blanket, camera on his shoulder, while being dragged across the floor. This delightful, deeply humanistic portrait of grassroots DIY cinema has all the charm and idiosyncrasies of a Jared Hess comedy.

5. Lost in La Mancha (2002)

Terry Gilliam was happy to have documentary makers Keith Fulton and Louis Pepe on set for The Man Who Killed Don Quixote after being impressed by The Hamster Factor, their behind-the-scenes film on the making of his earlier 12 Monkeys. The anguished result shows exactly why Quixote was abandoned after six days’ shooting in Spain in September 2000. Takes were rendered unusable by the roar of F16s from a nearby Nato base; Jean Rochefort, co-lead opposite Johnny Depp, fell seriously ill; and the equipment was destroyed by a merciless storm. Gilliam’s on-set catchphrase sums it up: “We’re fucked!” (When Quixote was eventually made in 2018, Fulton and Pepe documented that shoot, too, in He Dreams of Giants.)

4. Henri-Georges Clouzot’s Inferno (2009)

The subgenre of documentaries about unfinished films stretches back to the BBC’s 1965 The Epic That Never Was, which investigated Josef von Sternberg’s planned version of I, Claudius starring Charles Laughton and Merle Oberon. But it reached its apotheosis with Henri-Georges Clouzot’s Inferno, Ruxandra Medrea and Serge Bromberg’s ravishing reflection on an early-1960s Proustian psychological drama from the director of Les Diaboliques. Lavishly funded by Columbia, Clouzot’s vision was impossibly ambitious, with three crews and a trippy array of complicated in-camera special effects. The director, who could not be dissuaded from shooting time-consuming test footage, suffered a heart attack three weeks into the 18-week shoot. The fragments of his vision, cherrypicked here from 15 hours of unseen footage, are intoxicating: where else can you see Romy Schneider covered in glitter, cellophane and olive oil?

3. Burden of Dreams (1982)

Deep in the rainforests of South America, Werner Herzog battles mud and misery, along with his leading man Klaus Kinski, to make Fitzcarraldo, about one man’s dream of building an opera house in the Amazon. Les Blank’s documentary, which is arguably more compelling than the movie it’s about, enables us to watch in disbelief as a film about a lunatic mission turns into one itself. Herzog’s initial footage has to be abandoned when the lead actor, Jason Robards, falls ill with amoebic dysentery and co-star Mick Jagger is needed on a world tour. Up and running again, the production is forced to relocate more than 1,000 miles away due to a border war, while Herzog’s plans to move a steamship up a hillside provide a textbook example of madness eclipsing method.

2. American Movie (1999)

Mark Borchardt, a Milwaukee junkyard poet with a mullet and plateglass specs, may be best suited to factory work or serial killing, according to his brother, but he positively glows with a passion for cinema. Lacking the funds to finish his feature debut, he instead tries to complete a short horror film, Coven, undaunted by his inability to pronounce the title. More Wiseau than Welles, he has optimism and indefatigability to burn. Not to mention a crew of colourful collaborators, including his mother, whom he enlists as an extra despite her protestations that she needs to go shopping; his bleary, poodle-haired pal and former acid-head Mike; and the gnarled, trailer-dwelling Uncle Bill, who needs 30 takes to deliver four lines. Director Chris Smith (who later made the priceless Fyre festival documentary) rightly portrays Mark as one of cinema’s most inspiring heroes – even if he still hasn’t finished his first feature.

1. Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker’s Apocalypse (1991)

Megadoc, the forthcoming behind-the-scenes film about Francis Ford Coppola’s $120m passion project Megalopolis, is directed by Mike Figgis, though earlier Coppola-related documentaries tended to be family affairs. The director’s late wife, Eleanor, was responsible for Making Marie Antoinette, released later this month, about their daughter Sofia’s 2006 historical fantasia. And it was Eleanor, too, who co-directed the extraordinary Hearts of Darkness, which draws on her 60 hours of footage and 40 hours of audio recordings, as well as her own diaries, all from the turbulent 238-day shooting of Apocalypse Now. The film reveals her husband arguing on set with Dennis Hopper, frantically typing new scenes just moments before the cameras roll, and negotiating with Marlon Brando, who has piled on the pounds but neglected to learn his lines. “I’m thinking of shooting myself,” the director confides. “This is one crisis I can’t pull myself out of.”

Boorman and the Devil is in cinemas in the UK and Ireland now. Making Marie Antoinette is in cinemas in the UK, Ireland and US from 23 October and streaming on Mubi from 6 November

BreakingNewsTab.title: Dual UK-Iranian national arrested over RAF Fairford incident
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A UK-Iranian dual national has been arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with the incident at RAF Fairford, counter-terror police have said.

The 27-year-old man was arrested in Westminster, London. A second man, a 26-year-old UK national, has also been questioned under caution, and two properties in the area have been searched.

Five men in their twenties who were arrested near the Gloucestershire airbase on Sunday remain on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London.

Counter-terror police are considering "all possible angles - including foreign state involvement", the force's senior national coordinator Vicki Evans said.

"The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry," she said.

"I'd like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this investigation."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday there were "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident. He did not provide further details, and Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

The five men were arrested in the early hours of Sunday morning after "three suspicious vehicles" were reported travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident.

The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

Police said a quantity of petrol but no explosive devices were found during searches of vans near the site.

The group were aged between 23 and 25. Four live in Westminster and one in Camden, and searches of their homes were carried out.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that "the hands of a foreign actor" had clearly been involved in the incident at the base, which has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades.

In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the airbase for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Flight attacker 'underwent Islamist radical indoctrination', Netanyahu says
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".

The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely.

Speaking to Fox News, Netanyahu also said it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane".

Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) state news agency reports investigations have begun there to determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose".

The co-pilot is currently being questioned in Saudi Arabia, where the plane made an emergency landing. However UAE officials say they have jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft on which the attack took place is registered there and flies under its flag.

Netanyahu told Fox that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal that's not a question".

"And with all the passengers in there, and if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think ... that'll give us a pretty good clue but again I don't make final conclusions yet but that's the indications we have now."

The prime minister was also asked earlier on the same network whether there was an indication if Iran was involved, he replied: "It's too early to say".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Hundreds of criminals leave prison under early release scheme
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Hundreds of criminals are being released early from prisons in England and Wales under new rules introduced to prevent facilities reaching capacity.

The first 700 of an expected 4,500 inmates eligible under the scheme were due to be let out on Thursday.

The government has stressed they will remain subject to strict monitoring arrangements, including the expanded use of electronic tagging, and has said action was needed to prevent prisons from becoming full.

But the plan has been strongly criticised by victims and questions have been raised over whether the Probation Service has sufficient resources to monitor thousands more criminals in the community.

Prisons in England and Wales are a matter of months away from reaching capacity, with Ministry of Justice data showing as of Monday 87,499 people were incarcerated, taking prison population levels up to 98.2%.

Thursday's release is the first of 10 scheduled to take place, with the final slated for June 2027.

Prisoners released initially were serving sentences of up to 19 months, with the most serious offenders - serving fixed sentences of more than 12 years - leaving in later waves.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Treasury minister James Murray said: "I know the level of concern and maybe anger will be intense, and it's worth me making clear that this is not a situation where there is any good solution - there's just a series of very difficult choices we've got to take."

He said the government "inherited a prison system on the brink" and without early releases the country would face a situation where "people who are arrested now can't go behind bars".

Murray said measures were in place to restrict criminals' movements in the community, adding: "I can't guarantee exactly what will happen, but I can tell people we have done everything we can to reduce the amount of people being released as far possible."

An early release programme introduced by the Conservatives saw more than 10,000 prisoners freed early between October 2023 and September 2024.

Sir Keir Starmer's government introduced the Sentencing Act to deal with the ongoing capacity crisis, which stipulated that offenders who were due to spend 40% or 50% of their sentences in prison would leave after a third - while prisoners who previously served two thirds would leave after half.

The number of people expected to be released under this scheme was cut from around 6,000 after Prime Minister Andy Burnham intervened to review its terms, removing eligibility for crimes including all forms of manslaughter, grooming offences and causing or allowing the death of a child.

The scheme does not apply to indeterminate sentences, which are handed out for the most serious offences like murder, and require a parole board to deem a prisoner safe to be released.

London Victims' Commissioner Andrea Simon said the exemptions "have not included some offenders whose imminent release is a genuinely terrifying prospect for their victims".

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "[There is] no real reason to believe that an even shorter spell in prison will have dealt with the risk that their offender poses."

Simon also questioned whether electronic tagging would be an effective safeguard, saying the equipment "will tell you where someone is but it can't stop them from doing something they shouldn't be doing".

Earlier this week, the Chief Inspector of Probation Martin Jones said the electronic monitoring regime had "not kept pace" and could create "a false sense of assurance" unless failing are addressed.

Some newly released prisoners spoke to the BBC as they were freed, including former bus driver Michael Bogle - who described the conditions inside London's Wandsworth Prison as "awful".

"Tagging is better than prison," he told reporters in support of the early release scheme. But others said they were concerned about a lack of support awaiting them on the outside, while one man told the BBC he did not know he was being released until Thursday morning.

Kirsty Pellant is among victims whose perpetrator was expected to be released in the coming months.

A man was convicted of several offences against her, including stalking, and jailed for five years in January 2025 after she discovered her photograph had been used to create a fake identity online and portray her as a sex worker.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she had received assurances he would not be let out in the first wave of releases but was not told when he would be.

The uncertainty "leaves us in such a dangerous position as victims because we need to be prepared, we need to know what we're dealing with," she added.

Prisoners released early can immediately be returned to prison if they breach the terms of their licence, including by committing another crime, contacting a victim or living at an address not approved by authorities.

However, charities have raised concerns that domestic abuse survivors may still be put at risk, despite such provisions.

"We know that license conditions are frequently breached by perpetrators", the charity Refuge warned, and cautioned that it was "deeply concerned that newly released perpetrators will be able to continue their campaign of abuse" without proper enforcement.

Women's Aid chief executive Farah Nazeer meanwhile said the scheme could further erode "incredibly low" trust in the criminal justice system, meaning "even greater numbers of women and children may be left without protection".

Ministers have also introduced restrictions zones, which will allow the Probation Service - which monitors offenders after they leave prison - to stipulate they can only move within a small geographic area, limiting their chance of a victim coming into contact with them.

But the National Association of Probation Officers (Napo) trade union has warned the service is "significantly under-staffed", adding: "You cannot solve the prisons crisis unless probation is fully functioning and provides a real alternative to custody."

The union's general secretary Ian Lawrence questioned government pledges to increase probation staff to deal with the influx of released prisoners, telling the BBC he had "heard it all before".

Government projections indicate the prison population will still rise to around 100,000 by the end of the decade despite early release schemes.

Minister have pledged to invest £7bn in a prison building programme which will expand capacity by 14,000 cells by 2031.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Tennessee halts executions after Christa Pike survives two lethal injection attempts
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Executions in Tennessee have been halted for the rest of the year, Governor Bill Lee has said, after two attempts to execute death row inmate Christa Pike by lethal injection failed.

Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Lee said he was "highly disappointed" about the botched execution, which he called one of the state's "most serious responsibilities". He has ordered an independent review.

Tennessee prison officials on Wednesday attempted to administer two lethal doses of pentobarbital to Pike but she survived and was taken to hospital. Her medical condition is unclear.

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.

She was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer.

Pike would have been the first woman to be executed in Tennessee for over 200 years.

Lee said on Thursday the investigation into Pike's botched execution "will be thorough", adding that "it's going to take time".

"There are a lot of questions," Lee said. "The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered, and that's what this investigation is for."

Lee has not made clear who will conduct the independent review of the state's execution procedures.

His order to pause all executions will overlap with the planned 3 December execution of convicted murderer Gary Sutton.

In court filings, Pike's lawyers said she needed "life-saving measures" after her botched execution.

The Tennessee Department of Correction, which handled the execution, issued a statement defending its handling of the case.

It said in a statement that it "followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general's office".

"The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening."

Pike was given two doses of the chemical pentobarbital, as per state protocol when the first attempt fails, but was still alive afterwards, according to court filings.

"This execution is causing Ms Pike unnecessary agony and occurring in violation of his right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment," her lawyers said.

The Tennessee attorney general's office said in a statement that it agreed with the decision to call for an investigation, adding: "We need to know what happened."

Pike's attempted execution proceeded after multiple last-minute legal challenges by her lawyers had failed, overturned in the final hour by the US Supreme Court.

Slemmer's mother May Martinez, who was among those who wanted the execution to take place and who travelled to Tennessee to witness it, told NBC News after the botched attempt that "it was a mess".

US Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn, who is running for Tennessee governor, described the situation as "tragic".

"While there should be a thorough review of what happened and why the process failed, the answer is simple: bring back the electric chair," Blackburn said.

Democrat Jerri Green, Blackburn's opponent, criticised her for wanting to "bring back one of the most cruel forms of capital punishment".

"As governor, I would put a moratorium on all future executions," Green said on X.

This is the second time in 2026 Tennessee officials attempted and failed to execute a prisoner.

In May, the execution of Tony Carruthers was called off after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal drug. Carruthers was given a one-year reprieve.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Fires break out at French schools as students protest nationwide
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Fires have broken out at several schools in France, as students protest by blockading education institutions nationwide over school funding and studying conditions.

Blazes were reported at two high schools in Nantes, western France, while another was filmed engulfing the entrance to another in the northern city of Rouen.

Students are protesting about a lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. University students joined the demonstrations on Thursday, citing similar demands.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu held a crisis meeting on Thursday to discuss the unrest. The government said afterwards that the student-led demonstrations had descended into "urban violence".

Both fires in Nantes spread after a bin was set alight. The blaze at the Nelson Mandela high school, in the city centre, then spread to the front of the building, damaging the entrance hall.

In the southern city of Marseille, staff at Victor Hugo high school were splashed with petrol as protesters reportedly filled containers.

While in the north, a headteacher at Degrugillier high school, in the village of Auchel, was injured in the ear by a wayward firework.

The blockades and protests at French lycées - for 15-18 year olds and equivalent to sixth forms in the UK or high schools in the US - began last week before spreading to hundreds of schools across the country.

French media report 625 people were arrested on Wednesday alone while 83 police officers were injured. More than 600 arrests had been made by midday on Thursday, excluding Paris, broadcaster ICI reports.

At least 30 universities have also reportedly been blockaded, including campuses in Rennes and Paris.

On Thursday, public transport services in Marseille and Strasbourg were halted due vandalism, threats of violence and to hinder protesters from moving around.

Seventeen-year-old Raphael took part in protests outside a school in Strasbourg, where barriers were used to obstruct nearby tram tracks.

He voiced his frustration at his school's facilities in an interview with news agency AFP, saying some rooms had leaks and that there were not enough toilets.

"The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There's zero budget, zero resources, not enough supervisors," Raphael said.

While France's next general election is still months away, the protests and how French authorities are responding to them has been heavily politicised.

The government and hard-right politicians have blamed the hard left for igniting protests, which are being organised by a union representing lycée students.

Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of a Parisian suburb and member of the radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party defended earlier remarks in which he said violence could be legitimate in some cases - referencing cases in which protesters had allegedly been shot at while not wearing helmets or bulletproof vests.

LFI leader and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, meanwhile, stressed he was in favour of non-violent protests, while arguing that blaming the left would not solve the issues motivating the demonstrations.

Earlier, leader of the hard-right National Rally Marine Le Pen said: "This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organized by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise."

The presidential candidate called for a new anti-rioting law to be passed.

Left-wing mayor of Marseille Benoît Payan condemned the "unacceptable violence" in his city.

While young people were "legitimately concerned" about their future and public services, they must express themselves in a calm fashion, he said.

Eric Ciotti, the Republicans mayor of Nice, said the parents of those found to have damaged school property should be made to pay for the repairs.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Travelodge failed Maidenhead sex assault victim 'at every stage'
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A woman who was sexually assaulted by a man given a key to her hotel room was "fundamentally failed" by Travelodge "at every stage", an independent review has found.

Barrister Paul Greaney KC said the chain's security policies at the time of the attack at its Maidenhead hotel in December 2022 were "not fit for the purpose of keeping guests safe".

He found guests were still not as safe as they should be, with room intrusions reported at nearly one-in-10 Travelodge hotels this summer, and no policy in place on violence against women and girls.

Travelodge apologised "unreservedly" to the woman. The review did credit the company with making changes since March.

Kyran Smith, who obtained the key by falsely claiming to be the woman's boyfriend, was jailed for seven-and-a-half years in January.

The review found he was handed the key less than three minutes after approaching the reception desk, by a receptionist who had received no training in key security.

Greaney said blame rested with Travelodge, that has its HQ in Thame, Oxfordshire, as an organisation rather than with individual staff, and a culture had developed in which room intrusions were regarded as "one of those things".

The woman emailed a complaint to Travelodge in January 2023, addressed to chief executive Jo Boydell and others.

The review concluded the email was handled by her office without her knowledge, and did not come to Boydell's attention until March 2026.

The woman's complaint was instead investigated by a manager who was himself criticised in it, and the customer services team offered her a refund for her night's stay, which she understood to be £30.

Boydell stepped down as chief executive in August following criticism over the company's handling of safety complaints. The review said she deserved credit for driving improvements from March.

The attack became national news in March after the woman contacted the BBC, saying the case raised serious questions about room security at Travelodge hotels.

Since then, dozens of people have shared experiences of strangers entering their rooms, including a domestic abuse victim whose abuser was given a key to her room at a Travelodge in London.

Then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer wrote to Boydell in March urging her to "seriously engage" with the government over security. Greaney was appointed to lead the review the following month.

The review makes 38 recommendations, including moving towards a system that requires guests to show ID to get a room key, which Travelodge has been trialling at some hotels since May.

It also calls for body-worn cameras for reception staff, better checks that staff have understood their training, and for housekeepers to always send guests to reception.

Greaney said Travelodge must "urgently" create a policy on violence against women and girls, drawn up with the Suzy Lamplugh Trust, and train all staff in it.

The review said changes made this year had been done quickly "albeit years too late" and its new key security policy would prevent a repeat of the Maidenhead attack if applied correctly.

But it found the policy was "not being applied with anything like sufficient consistency on the ground".

Mystery shoppers were able to get into rooms through housekeeping staff at all five hotels tested, including Maidenhead, without being sent to reception or asked for proof they were entitled to enter.

At three of the hotels, staff confirmed a guest was staying there, and at two, room numbers were said out loud at check-in. The Maidenhead hotel scored worst of the five.

Other recommendations included networked CCTV across the chain and key card-controlled access to all residential corridors.

Greaney said room intrusions were a problem across the hotel sector.

He praised the woman's courage and determination, saying the problems would have remained "beneath the surface" had she not shared her experience.

Freddie van Mierlo, the Liberal Democrat MP for Henley and Thame, where Travelodge is based, said he was worried the company was "still trying to do safety on the cheap".

He said the review's recommendations would require "significant capital investment", and Travelodge needed to make clear it was prepared to deliver that.

In response, a Travelodge spokesperson said: "We are committed to implementing the recommendations and will make the necessary investments to do so.

"We cannot provide a specific figure but can assure people that all required investments in guest safety will be made and we have the resources required."

Ray Reidy, Travelodge's interim chief executive, said the review made clear there were failures in its policies and in the way customers had been treated.

"I apologise unreservedly on behalf of Travelodge to all guests where we have failed," he said.

"We have made significant progress in preventing and addressing these issues over the past six months, and we recognise we still have further to go."

Travelodge said a new board committee would oversee the changes, with independent assessments of its progress after six and 12 months.

BreakingNewsTab.title: UK in talks with EU partners to release strategic fuel reserves if needed, BBC understands
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Britain is in talks with EU partners to release additional strategic fuel reserves, including diesel, if needed, the BBC understands.

The talks come after President Donald Trump threatened to ban diesel exports from the US in a bid to reduce record prices at the pumps for Americans.

Diesel prices in the UK also hit record highs this week and are hovering just under 200p per litre, according to motoring organisation the RAC.

The US is a vital supplier of diesel to the world, exporting between 1.2 and 1.5 million barrels per day, with experts warning a ban on shipments abroad could put further pressure on prices in other countries.

"We're thinking about it very seriously," Trump said of an export ban at the weekend.

Energy Minister Martin McCluskey was on a call with European counterparts on Thursday to discuss the potential ban.

A source familiar with the discussions told the BBC it was prudent to prepare a co-ordinated response with other countries, including those across EU, but added that there were still European reserves left from a coordinated release of strategic fuel stocks earlier in the year.

"We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry," a government spokesperson said. The government has stressed that there is no cause for concern about potential diesel shortages, though prices are expected to rise further.

A European Commission spokesperson said today that there were "lots of calls, lots of meetings" taking place on the diesel situation, including with "high level contacts" in the US administration.

A meeting of the governing board of the International Energy Agency (IEA) is taking place tomorrow.

Prices of petrol and diesel globally have skyrocketed since the outbreak of the US-Israel war in Iran in February. The closure of the vital Strait of Hormuz, which typically transports around a fifth of the world's oil and gas, has pushed up the price of products made from oil.

An export ban from Russia, also a major supplier of diesel, has added to the pressure on prices.

Trump has argued that keeping any surplus barrels of diesel in the US would lower pump prices domestically, offering immediate relief to drivers, truckers, and businesses ahead of the midterm elections.

But David Fyfe, chief economist at Argus Media, said cutting off American supply would likely cause international prices to skyrocket.

Diesel prices have hit an all-time high in the UK, with the latest RAC figures showing average pump prices at 199.79p per litre, up from 142.38p

Diesel is harder to refine than gasoline and, because it is used by the haulage industry and in agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

The UK is heavily reliant on imports. Although the four refineries in the UK make more than enough petrol to meet demand, they do not make enough diesel for the country's needs.

There were 15.1 million diesel vehicles on UK roads at the end of June, according to the Department for Transport. That is a drop from 15.7 million a year before.

There were 9.8 million diesel cars, down year on year from 10.4 million.

BreakingNewsTab.title: What happened in the failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?
BreakingNewsTab.text:
US convicted murderer Christa Pike is in hospital and being given "life-saving measures" after Tennessee authorities failed in their attempt to execute her by lethal injection.

The case of Pike, whose attempted execution had already been the subject of a high-profile legal battle, has raised a number of questions.

These include what went wrong, what happens next, and - for opponents of the death penalty - fresh concerns around the suffering of an inmate when an execution does not go to plan.

A review into what happened has been ordered and executions in Tennessee have been halted for the rest of the year, Governor Bill Lee said.

The Tennessee Department of Correction defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening".

The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.

Authorities have yet to provide their explanation of why the dosage given to Pike proved to be non-fatal, although medical experts have provided theories of their own.

Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine, told the BBC he had been retained by Pike's legal team as a medical expert and that Pike probably never achieved a sufficient blood level of pentobarbital to cause her breath to stop or heart failure.

The state correction department added that Pike had been taken to an off-site medical facility.

One of her lawyers said she was "being provided life-saving measures" in hospital.

Her health status is unclear as of Thursday morning.

In his emailed comments to the BBC, Zivot said: "It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury."

A third-party review has been ordered by state Governor Bill Lee, who said on Thursday that Tennessee will halt executions for the rest of the year.

This could impact any additional attempt by the state to execute Pike in the near-term, if she does regain consciousness. Her current state is not clear.

May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer who had pushed for Pike's execution to take place, told NBC News the events had been "a mess".

Historically, the US Supreme Court has not halted second attempts at executions, said John Mills, an attorney who works with inmates sentenced to death.

In 2024, it allowed the state of Alabama to proceed with a second execution of Kenneth Eugene Smith, after their attempt to execute him by lethal injection failed two years before. Alabama used an experimental oxygen deprivation method to put Smith to death.

A notable Supreme Court case from 1947 allowed the state of Louisiana to attempt a second electrocution of Willie Smith, a black teenager whose first execution attempt failed when he was 17 years old.

The court found a second execution would not violate the Constitution's prohibitions against double jeopardy or cruel and unusual punishment, and Smith was executed aged 18.

"If the question is, is it likely the federal courts would intervene in a second attempt? I'm afraid the answer is a resounding no," Mills said of Pike's case.

Pike's lawyers have already filed a motion to stay her execution.

Mills said that if he was her lawyer, he would be asking the federal courts to reconsider their views on a second attempt and "would also be looking at the Tennessee constitution and ask the Tennessee courts to reconsider".

Mills added that he would also approach Governor Lee, who has powers to issue stays of executions and exercise clemency.

Opponents of the death penalty have been quick to react.

Maya Foa, the chief executive of international legal organisation Reprieve, said: "We cannot know exactly what went wrong, because so much happened behind a curtain – lethal injection relies on secrecy at every stage, to hide the violence of the state taking a human life."

Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. There is a historical precedent of authorities making a second attempt to execute those on death row.

Meanwhile Shipp, Pike's boyfriend and co-defendant, remains in prison, having been spared the death penalty under state law. He was 17 at the time that Slemmer was killed.

Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.

Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review - which took place under the presidency of Joe Biden - raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".

His government banned its use in federal executions but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods.

In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes.

The Tennessee Department of Correction has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded". Drugs may degrade for a number of reasons, including if it has aged beyond its use-by date and its potency has decreased.

The department issued a broader defence of its method, writing in a statement: "The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective."

Some manufacturers have explicitly said they will no longer produce pentobarbital or will restrict their use in executions, according to Alexis Hoag-Fordjor, Co-Director of the Center for Criminal Justice at Brooklyn Law School.

In 2024, for instance, the manufacturer Absolute Standards said it would no longer make the drug., external

"It's unclear, the quality and the effectiveness of the drug" used in Pike's execution, Hoag-Fordjor told the BBC, given how difficult it has been for states like Tennessee to obtain pentobarbital. "It shouldn't be a surprise something went wrong."

The predicament Tennessee authorities found themselves in - having to call emergency medical services to save Pike after trying to kill her - suggested there was "no plan in place" for a scenario like Pike's, Hoag-Fordjor said.

"It's just such a bizarre reality to continue with capital punishment."

The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.

The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal injection. He was given a one-year reprieve by Governor Bill Lee.

More widely across the US, the issue of botched executions continues to cause alarm.

In 2022, more than a third of executions in the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPI) - an organisation that provides statistics and research on the death penalty but does not take a stance on it morally.

The DPI says lethal injection has the high­est rate of botched exe­cu­tions.

An incident in Oklahoma in 2014 gained particular notoriety. The execution of Clayton Lockett was postponed after 20 minutes because the lethal injection of three drugs failed to work properly when one of his veins ruptured, and he went on to writhe and shake uncontrollably.

In the US, 27 of the 50 states have the death penalty under state law. The federal government can also carry out executions after President Donald Trump, a supporter of capital punishment, ended a moratorium last year, However, it is yet to actually carry out any executions since then.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Russian dissident Garry Kasparov says US warned him of danger to his life
BreakingNewsTab.text:
An exiled Russian opposition figure living in the US says he was warned by American and Lithuanian security services that his life was in danger.

Former chess world champion Garry Kasparov said he was one of two dissidents told to take precautions, which he had done.

His comments come after the US Justice Department unsealed an indictment earlier this month charging five people who allegedly work for a network linked to the Kremlin with plotting attacks and murders in countries including the US, focusing on Russian dissidents and defectors.

Kasparov wrote in his publication The Next Move that he had not been told explicitly that he and fellow Free Russia Forum co-founder Ivan Tyutrin were considered targets, but said both had been warned about their safety.

Spanish newspaper El Mundo reported that it had obtained information that Kasparov, along with another Russian opposition figure, Ilya Ponomarev, had been warned about the plot over the summer by US authorities.

Citing sources close to Kasparov, the paper said he had been placed under enhanced protection over the summer for the first time since he moved to the US.

Kasparov wrote separately: "I will not stop and I will not hide, even if I thought it was possible to do so.

"My family and I will not truly be safe as long as [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is in power in Russia - a circumstance shared by millions."

Kasparov retired from competitive chess in 2005 to pursue a career in politics, founding movements that openly opposed Putin before fleeing Russia in 2013.

He has not returned since. Russia classed him as a foreign agent following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and subsequently added him to a list of terrorists and extremists in 2024 - both categorisations he rejects.

The other reported target, Ponomarev, was the only Russian MP who voted against the illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 and later went into exile in Ukraine.

He declined to confirm or deny to the Moscow Times whether he had been tipped off about the alleged plot but said the allegations marked "a new level of escalation" by Russia.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Japan raises permanent residency fees for foreigners by 20 times
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Japan has raised fees for foreigners seeking permanent residency in the country by 20 times to 200,000 yen ($1,270; £955).

Those seeking permanent residency must now also meet new income, pension and Japanese-language requirements.

Long lines formed outside immigration offices earlier this week as applicants sought to beat the fee hikes, with Tokyo's main immigration bureau reporting wait times of over seven hours.

The fee increases are part of a series of changes to Japan's immigration policy under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, which aim to manage its rapidly growing foreign population.

In July, Japan implemented a five-fold increase in visa fees for all foreigners – its first visa fee hike in 50 years. Authorities said this was meant to "reflect inflation and exchange rate fluctuations".

Although immigration remains politically sensitive and restrictive in Japan, the nation's ageing population is increasingly relying on foreign workers to plug a labour shortage.

Japan's foreign resident population surpassed 4.12 million at the end of 2025, marking a record 9.5% increase from the previous year. This however has led to growing anxieties over immigration and social change.

Takaichi has made managing immigration one of her key priorities since she took office in October last year.

In an X post days before the residency permit hikes set in, Takaichi wrote that her government recognises that "some members of the public may feel a sense of concern or unfairness" as Japan's foreign resident population grows.

"To address these concerns, [the government] is working to ensure that its policies toward foreign nationals are orderly, and that both Japanese citizens and foreign residents can live safely and securely," she wrote.

Before the hikes, it would cost non-permanent residents in Japan 6,000 yen each time they applied to change their residency status or extend their period of stay.

From 1 October, the fee varies according to the duration of stay sought – from 10,000 yen for three months or less, to 75,000 yen for five years or more.

Applicants who face financial hardship or are designated as refugees would be granted discounts.

Aspiring permanent residents must now also earn a stable income at or above the Japanese average. Latest data released in July puts average household income at 5.75 million yen as of 2024.

Micaiah Stevens, who has been living and working in Tokyo for 10 years, was not able to compile the necessary documentation to submit his application for permanent residency before the price hike.

The 37-year-old still plans to apply, but questions the new measures aimed at foreign residents.

"My immediate reaction was that foreigners were being treated a bit too conveniently. We're being asked to make more than the average Japanese person, pay a significantly higher fee, just to be able to work in Japan and provide taxes," he tells the BBC.

"There's already a significant language and cultural barrier that prevents some talent from coming over. This just doesn't strike me as a plan that was thought out to the long term."

From April next year, permanent residency applicants will face even tighter requirements, including basic Japanese language proficiency. This has led to a surge in enrollments at Japanese language schools as well as people signing up to take the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test, local media reported.

Applicants' expected pension benefits must also be equivalent to that of someone who has enrolled into the employee pension system for 30 years, although the value of one's financial assets can be considered if their expected pension benefits fall short.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Renee Good: Family of US woman killed by ICE agent sues Trump officials
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The family of a woman who was killed by an immigration agent in Minneapolis in January has announced two lawsuits against the US government and members of the Trump administration.

Renee Good, a US citizen, was shot to death by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer during a major immigration sweep. Millions watched the video recorded of her killing and residents of the Minnesota city took to the streets to protest.

One lawsuit blames the government for her death, claiming the operation created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence", a lawyer for the family said.

The BBC has contacted the White House and Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

The lawsuits were brought by Good's brother, Brent Ganger, and her partner, Becca Good.

Speaking publicly for the first time since the shooting, Becca Good told a news conference on the lawsuits on Thursday: "The whole world had to watch as our entire universe was destroyed."

"We were all robbed," she said as she described how the shooting affected their three children.

In one of the lawsuits, the family accuses the government of "battery, assault, false imprisonment, intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligence that caused Renee's death".

It cites the Federal Tort Claims Act, which allows citizens to sue the government for personal injury, death, or property damage caused by the negligence of federal employees.

The second lawsuit targets ICE officer Jonathan Ross, who shot Good, as well as White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House border chief Tom Homan and others, alleging a "conspiracy to interfere with civil rights by senior federal officials, federal immigration enforcement agents, and private actors".

"Our government has become a grave and mortal threat to its own citizens," the family's lawyer, Antonio Romanucci said at the news conference.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Algeria introduces death penalty for arsonists after wildfires
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Algeria has adopted a law imposing the death penalty on people convicted of arson of forests or fields after a series of deadly wildfires swept parts of the country.

Members of the national assembly voted through the bill, which also made child abduction a capital offence, on Thursday.

Capital punishment has been in the country's penal code for some offences, but no execution has been carried out since 1993.

The official death toll from the blazes stands at 12, but independent news outlets believe the figure to be much higher.

Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune ordered the justice ministry to introduce the changes to the criminal law after more than 100 fires in the north-east of the country during an intense heatwave in northern Africa.

Under the law, anyone convicted of deliberately setting fire to forests, woods or fields could face execution.

The death penalty has also been extended to child kidnappings that involve torture, sexual assault or mutilation.

According to news agency AFP, Justice Minister Lotfi Boudjemaa told parliament: "The adoption of the death penalty for these acts is the appropriate legal response to curb these crimes."

The tougher penalties were justified because arson had reached "the level of organised crime", with investigations suggesting links to "foreign parties", Boudjemaa said.

The upper house, the Council of the Nation, will review the law before it is officially ratified by the president.

Investigative journalist Nozha Khelalef has been gathering the names of those believed to have died in the fires from death notices posted by families and information shared by some local authorities.

Her tally, listed on the independent news website Twala, external, puts the death toll at 200.

While Algeria regularly experiences forest fires in the summer, climate change has exacerbated the intensity and severity of recent wildfires in the country.

FinanceTab.title: Vape tax comes into force with prices set to rise
FinanceTab.text:
The price of vapes is set to rise as a new tax comes into effect, with the aim of making vaping less attractive to children and young people.

The Vaping Product Duty will be imposed at a rate of £2.20 per 10ml of e-liquid. However, many customers will not see a jump in prices immediately, as sellers have six months to sell old stock at the pre-duty price.

The government wants to reduce the appeal of vapes by making them more expensive, as more evidence of its adverse effect on health comes out, particularly on children and young people.

The vaping industry has lobbied against the new tax, saying that affordable vapes help people to quit smoking.

The duty will apply to all vaping products regardless of whether they contain nicotine.

Tobacco rates were also raised on Thursday, by £2.20 per 100 cigarettes or 50g of tobacco. HMRC said this maintains the financial incentive for smokers to switch to vaping.

HMRC is also launching a stamp for vaping products which are traceable throughout the supply chain.

All vapes sold in the UK must carry this stamp from April.

The new tax is also an effort to combat illicit trade, which is a growing problem on UK high streets. Last month, the prime minister announced new powers for councils that will address the decline of the high street, including the amount of vape shops.

Changes to planning law in England mean every new shop selling e-cigarettes, or vapes, would need to apply to their local council for permission to open.

Health Minister Karin Smyth said: "These measures are an important step in our ambition to tackle youth vaping by reducing the affordability of vaping products, which goes hand-in-hand with the work we are already doing to tackle the appeal and availability of vapes on our high streets."

James Murray, the Financial Secretary to the Treasury, said the government was "backing all those retailers who play by the rules".

John Dunne, the director general of the UK Vaping Industry Association, said: "This is nothing short of a tax on public health."

He said vapes had helped "millions of adults cut down on or stop smoking".

"Protecting young people is essential. But that means stronger enforcement against illegal and rogue traders, not making legal vaping more expensive for adults trying to stay away from cigarettes."

Experts say vaping is much safer than smoking, but it is not risk free and the long-term effects are less clear.

A recent review of vaping studies found that it had an association with problems in children and young people including wheezing and coughing, poor oral and dental health, poor sleep, mental health problems and eye symptoms.

The NHS has said that children and non-smokers should never vape.

Additional reporting by Neranjana Elapatha

FinanceTab.title: Employers should teach primary-age children about work, Milburn says
FinanceTab.text:
Children should be introduced to the world of work at the start of primary school, says the author of a major report into youth activity in the UK.

Former minister Alan Milburn says children as young as four should be learning about different careers, with work experience placements made mandatory for 14- to 16-year-olds.

However, teaching unions warn of the "significant pressure" already facing primary schools and say practical considerations must ensure all schools have access to the support.

The latest data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) suggests 981,000 people aged 16 to 24 in the UK were not in education, employment or training (known as Neet), between April and June 2026.

Milburn told the BBC "in primary school, it's really about opening their eyes and giving them a sense about what is possible".

Despite a push towards apprenticeships and work experience in Years 10 and 11, for many the journey towards becoming Neet starts well before their 16th birthday.

As a result, Milburn says children should be introduced to the world of work much earlier in their school journey, with dedicated space in the curriculum to "broaden horizons".

He told the BBC this could be achieved by employers giving talks in primary schools and offering taster sessions to children.

"It'd be good if employers came into schools and said, 'Look, this is what's going on, these are things that are possible.'"

Milburn says that for Key Stage 4 pupils - aged between 14 and 16 - experience must be given in a real workplace with employer feedback.

"Work experience needs to be mandatory. It makes a big difference," he told the BBC.

Milburn also emphasised the difficulty some young people face when trying to find work experience placements.

"There are about four in ten people aged 14-16 who aren't getting any work experience at all," he said. "In other schools, students are told to go off and find their own work experience and that often relies on the network of Mum and Dad."

These recommendations are due to be published in the final instalment of his government-commissioned report into the issue, which is expected to be published in the autumn.

Education is devolved in the UK, so while Milburn's review looks at the picture in all four nations, his recommendations regarding education are specific to England.

Currently in England, careers guidance must be offered to students aged 11-18 and work experience is not statutory.

The government has said its vision, external is to "guarantee two weeks' worth of work experience for every young person" in England.

In both Scotland and Wales, career-based learning is already a requirement in schools for students as young as three.

FinanceTab.title: Energy bills are rising by £60 a year - here's how you can bring that down
FinanceTab.text:
Energy prices have now risen by nearly 4%, with forecasts of a much bigger jump to come in January.

It means a rise of about £60 per year – or £5 per month – taking an annual bill to £1,723 for the typical household using both electricity and gas.

Regulator Ofgem's price cap affects about 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales and sets a maximum price for each unit of gas and electricity.

Further increases are likel in January, with forecasters predicting a 16% increase, due to high wholesale prices paid by suppliers as a result of the conflict in the Middle East.

While that's beyond your control, here are four things you can do to help keep a check on rising bills.

The energy regulator, Ofgem, is advising people to consider fixing - so that the price you are charged per unit of gas or electricity does not change every three months, although the total bill will still vary depending on how much energy you use.

The trouble is that it is very difficult to work out whether a fixed deal is a good deal at the moment.

Should energy prices rise sharply, then those who have fixed already have the certainty of what they will pay for each unit of energy. That price may well be lower than the forecast price in January.

However, if events in the Gulf region settle down, and a peace deal in the Iran war leads to lower international gas prices, then a longer-term fix might not seem such good value compared with the price cap.

So consumer group Which? also recommends keeping an eye on any exit fees when picking a fixed deal. If variable prices fall below your fixed rate and you want to get out of it before the end of your agreement period, you may have to pay a hefty sum.

Before you fix, consumer website MoneySavingExpert advises you look at all the deals available, not just what your own supplier is offering.

Ofgem says about five million people still pay their bill when it arrives every three months. For some that's because they do not want their supplier to estimate their usage in case they are overcharged.

Taking regular meter readings, or having a smart meter, while paying by monthly direct debit solves that problem. Moreover, paying by direct debit costs less per unit than by so-called standard credit.

You will usually - although not always - need to switch to direct debit if you want to take advantage of the fixed deals on offer.

Customers on prepayment schemes - usually people on low incomes struggling to pay bills - used to pay a higher rate than others, but now they pay slightly less than the capped direct debit variable rate.

There are also a range of pricing schemes offering cheaper off-peak electricity, for example if you are charging an electric car overnight.

There are a range of ways people on low incomes can access support.

This winter anyone on means-tested benefits will get £150 off their electricity bill.

Your supplier will apply the discount automatically unless you are in Scotland, where you will need to contact your energy company to ask for the help.

Some people will also be eligible for a Cold Weather Payment, external and most pensioners will receive the winter fuel payment, after political pressure forced the government to U-turn on its plan to restrict it to the poorest pensioners.

Beyond that, most energy suppliers offer hardship grants for people struggling to pay their bills and the government's Fuel Direct Scheme, external can help you repay energy debt.

You can get more advice from Ofgem, external, Citizens Advice, external, or your own energy supplier. Trade body Energy UK has a list of support schemes, external.

People on low incomes may also be eligible for grants to help with insulating their homes, and there are local schemes offering grants for solar panels, heat pumps and the like.

But if you are hunting around for grants, watch out for scams pretending to be official money-off schemes.

Once the temperature outside starts to fall again, it is important to stay warm, especially for the very young, old, and those with health conditions or reduced mobility.

But there are plenty of ways you can keep bills lower without letting the temperature in your home fall below the recommended 18C minimum.

You may already have hung thicker curtains and blocked the draughts over the last couple of winters, but do not forget to switch off radiators in rooms you are not using and wrap up.

MoneySavingExpert advises to "heat the human not the home".

Turning down the flow rate on a combi boiler can save you money as often the water is being heated higher than it needs to be.

Batch cooking and using an air fryer or microwave rather than heating up the oven for a small item can save energy.

Take shorter showers and wash clothes at 30C rather than 40C. Dry clothes outdoors if you can, rather than using a tumble dryer, or hang clothes indoors but ventilate well or use a dehumidifier to avoid damp.

If you are thinking about moving home, or undertaking renovations, it is worth thinking through how to reduce bills. When it comes to white goods, look for energy-efficient appliances.

FinanceTab.title: Household energy bills forecast to see biggest rise in four years
FinanceTab.text:
Household energy prices are set to soar in January, with a typical annual bill forecast to jump by £276, figures shared with the BBC reveal.

The 16% predicted increase would hit millions of households at the coldest time of year, and would mark the biggest rise in bills for four years.

The forecast from consultancy Cornwall Insight comes a day before prices go up under regulator Ofgem's October price cap and puts increased pressure on the government to support those who will struggle to pay.

Meanwhile, the boss of supplier EDF Simone Rossi has warned the UK is "walking into a second energy crisis" and called for an extension to the VAT cut on electricity which kicks in on Thursday.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told BBC Radio 4's Today programme he would not call Rossi's crisis warning an overstatement, adding that the cost of home energy, as well as petrol and diesel, was "very difficult indeed".

Speaking from the Labour conference in Liverpool, he added: "We're looking at any measure that can give people breathing space, that can take the pressure off."

About 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales are on variable energy tariffs set by Ofgem's price cap, which puts a maximum price on each unit of gas and electricity.

Those homes will see a 4% increase in prices on Thursday, the equivalent of about £60 per year – or £5 per month – taking an annual bill to £1,723 for the typical household using both electricity and gas and paying by direct debit if this level was sustained for a year.

That rise would have been higher without the government's VAT cut, which knocks the equivalent of about £45 a year off a typical bill.

But forecasts show a far greater increase is possible for bills in January. Cornwall Insight said its latest forecast suggests the typical annual bill would rise to £1,999.

The forecast 16% rise will come at the worst time of year, according to Craig Lowrey, principal consultant at Cornwall Insight.

"These prices are going to hit households hard. January is already a difficult month for many, with cold weather and bank balances still recovering from Christmas," he said.

The predicted rise is the result of disruption of gas supplies owing to the conflict in the Middle East, and the resulting low gas storage levels in Europe. Rebuilding those stocks could mean high bills "well beyond the winter", the forecaster said.

Cornwall Insight has a strong track record on forecasts and is widely respected across the industry and politics. Similar forecasts have been made by energy suppliers.

This remains only a prediction at this stage. Ofgem will not announce the actual January price change until late November.

While an easing of tensions in the Middle East could lessen the pain for billpayers, the price setting period for the January cap is already halfway through.

With little sign of a truce or lower international energy costs, a big increase in prices for those not on a fixed tariff looks highly likely. Lowrey said a January rise was "all but certain".

That will be tough for people like Aaron Richards from Maidenhead.

"I try to eat less takeaways, work more overtime, and try to budget a bit better, but at the same time, we shouldn't have to," he said.

Aaron drives a diesel car, and so is paying record high prices to travel to and from work.

"I just feel like everything's going up. How far is it going to go? Someone's got to step in," he said.

"I know people who can't afford to heat their house and they're struggling at the moment. Housing and eating are two of life's essentials that everyone should have. It shouldn't be a challenge to have any of those things."

Among others calling for government help for struggling billpayers is Simone Rossi, chief executive of supplier EDF Energy.

Speaking exclusively to the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast, Mr Rossi said: "We are actually walking into a second significant energy crisis after the one we experienced just four years ago."

He said that the government should extend the cut in VAT on electricity bills from 5% to 0% beyond April, when it is due to expire.

He also urged ministers to give the go-ahead to the new Jackdaw gas field off the coast of Aberdeen, and the Rosebank oil field off Shetland.

The government has consistently said that it will consider ways to offer breathing space to billpayers on the cost of living.

Additional reporting by Oliver Smith and Paul Seddon. Graphics by Miguel Roca-Terry.

FinanceTab.title: Greggs to shut four factories and cut 740 jobs
FinanceTab.text:
High street bakery brand Greggs has announced plans to shut four of its factories and cut 740 jobs.

It plans to close manufacturing sites at North Lakes near Penrith, Cumbria, Pettigrews in Kelso, Scotland, Seaham in County Durham and Enfield, Greater London, though distribution operations would continue to run from the latter.

The proposals will also impact manufacturing operations at its Treforest site in Wales, but this will also continue as a distribution centre for the business.

The chain, which has headquarters in Newcastle, said its retail shops would not be affected by the proposed changes and like-for-like sales had grown across its managed stores.

It said the plans would save it about £20m across the 2028 and 2029 financial years.

The changes would take place over the next two and a half years, with parts of Greggs' manufacturing processes relocating, the firm said.

The range of products manufactured at its Clydesmill Glasgow and Manchester locations would be reduced and production of tinned bread at Gosforth would be stopped.

Some products would also be sourced from specialist suppliers.

The general secretary of the Bakers, Food and Allied Workers Union (BFAWU) Sarah Woolley said the union was "deeply concerned" about the announcement.

She said: "Our immediate priority is our members, their jobs, their families and the communities that could be affected by these proposals."

She added Greggs was clear in its own announcement the business continued to "perform strongly".

Greggs said positive trading and continued cost control means it expected a "modestly improved outcome" for 2026.

Like-for-like sales grew by 3.4% across its managed stores, with overall growth buoyed by the opening of new shops.

Woolley said Greggs' workers had played a "huge part" in getting the company where it is.

She said: "Against that backdrop, our members will understandably be asking why their jobs and livelihoods should now be put at risk in the name of efficiency and future progression."

But chief executive Roisin Currie said the company needed to "keep evolving alongside changing customer expectations".

She said: "Greggs manufacturing and logistics network remains a key strength of the business, and these proposals are intended to strengthen our manufacturing network, improve efficiency and ensure we remain well placed for the future while continuing to deliver the quality, value and service our customers expect."

The firm employs 33,000 people in the UK, the majority working in its stores.

A consultation with staff is expected to start soon and the company said "no final decisions" had been made yet.
