FinanceTab.title: Oura pulls $15bn stock market listing days after announcement
FinanceTab.text:
Oura has pulled its plan to sell shares in its business on the US stock market, in a move which would have valued the firm at $15bn (£11.3bn), just days after announcing it.

The maker of smart rings which track their owners' health said it would postpone its flotation "due to uncertainty in the Initial Public Offering (IPO) market" and did not say when it might go ahead.

Oura had filed official documents setting out plans to raise up to $2.2bn by offering shares in the business to investors just over a week ago.

The tech firm has become the latest business to delay its public listing, with experts saying the IPO market is getting more challenging.

Oura's chief executive Tom Hale said "an IPO is just one step in our journey", adding that "we have the luxury of choosing our moment".

Earlier this month, US nuclear technology firm Holtec International also postponed its flotation. It blamed an "unusual confluence of developments that has impaired investor confidence in the market for new public offerings".

In particular, it cited rising energy costs, military conflicts, global trade tensions and concerns about inflation which have led to central banks including the US Federal Reserve raising benchmark interest rates.

This week, the yield – or interest rate – on US debt repayable in 10 years' time hit the highest level since 2007.

Samuel Kerr, global head of equity capital markets at Mergermarket, said: "What is now clear is we are in a very different IPO market to the one we envisaged just a few weeks ago."

Oura had planned to sell shares priced at between $40 and $44 on the Nasdaq stock market index, giving the company an implied market value of $15bn.

In its last full financial year, ending 30 September 2025, Oura made a pre-tax profit of $23.5m on sales $907.8m. That compares to a $6.2m pre-tax profit in the previous year.

Its most recent figures for the nine months to 30 June this year show pre-tax income of $70m on sales of $1.2bn.

Oura, founded in Finland in 2013, has its global headquarters in San Francisco and makes smart rings – costing upwards of $300 – which monitor things such as its owner's heartbeat and sleep patterns which are analysed and presented on an app.

The company is the subject of a class action lawsuit which accused it of false advertising by claiming its rings can accurately track a person's sleep activity and patterns.

The lawsuit, filed by the Clarkson Law Firm in August, claimed: "Oura rings cannot measure one's sleep or cycles. That's because sleep happens in the brain, not on one's finger."

It is understood that Oura's decision to delay an IPO is not connected to the lawsuit.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Oura said: "We stand behind our science, research and accuracy claims."

They added: "Like other consumer sleep wearables, Oura Ring estimates sleep stages using multiple physiological signals, including heart rate, heart rate variability, movement, breathing patterns, and temperature."

FinanceTab.title: Brit Awards boosted Manchester economy by £5m, study finds
FinanceTab.text:
The Brit Awards' move to Manchester for the 2026 ceremony generated £5 million for the city and its surrounding area, research has found.

The annual awards ceremony, widely regarded as the UK's biggest night in music, was hosted in city for the first time this year after being held in the capital for its near 50-year history.

The move had a positive economic and social impact and created more than 3,000 temporary jobs, according to an independent study conducted by Amion Consulting.

Greater Manchester mayor Bev Craig praised the awards' move north as a "massive moment for our city region", with the 2027 event also set to be held in the city.

The show took place at Manchester's Co-op Live arena on 28 February in a ceremony hosted by comedian Jack Whitehall, and featuring performances from stars including Harry Styles, Olivia Dean, Raye and Mark Ronson.

It generated £5m in net additional expenditure in Manchester, with £3.6m coming from visitors and £1.4m as a result of organiser and partner expenditure.

Craig said the decision to hold the event in Manchester "was a recognition not only of our unmatched music heritage, but our growing reputation for putting on national and global events and making a success of them".

She said such events brought millions of pounds into Manchester's economy, boosting the culture and hospitality industries and created opportunities for people.

"We've done it once in style, and we'll do it again next year," she said, adding she was excited to help make 2027 an even bigger year for the Brits.

Manchester City Council leader Garry Bridges said this year's award show was "phenomenally successful".

"The partnership between the Brits and Manchester went so much further – with a massive social and economic reach right across the city and into our communities, which is still being felt now," he added.

FinanceTab.title: US borrowing costs hit 24-year high as global bond sell-off intensifies
FinanceTab.text:
The global bond sell-off intensified on Thursday, driving 10-year US government borrowing costs to their highest level in 24 years in a frantic day’s trading.

The threat of a renewed round of inflation from the persistently high cost of oil has spooked investors on both sides of the Atlantic, with central banks expected to raise interest rates in the coming months to prevent price increases from becoming embedded.

The sell-off drove the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year US Treasuries to 5.34% – the highest level since 2002.

In the UK, where surging borrowing costs are increasing the pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget later this month, the yield on 30-year bonds hit 6% for the first time since 1998, before easing slightly later in the day. Yields on five- and 10-year UK bonds were also up.

Stock market investors sold heavily too, knocking almost 1.7% off the FTSE 100 in London – its worst daily fall since May. Bourses in other parts of Europe were also hit, with Germany’s DAX falling 1% and France’s CAC 40 losing 1.6%.

“There is carnage in the bond market, which is hitting stocks hard,” said Neil Wilson, the investor strategist at Saxo UK. “It looks like the relentless rout in the bond market is sending investors running for cover.”

The bond sell-off around the world is being driven by fears of high inflation, as the Middle East conflict continues to restrict oil supplies from the region.

Japan’s 10-year yield rose towards the 30-year high set last month.

US bonds weakened despite inflation data on Wednesday coming in lower than forecast, which was expected to calm investors’ nerves about the prospect of further increases in the cost of borrowing by the US Federal Reserve.

Traders remain anxious that the Fed will continue to raise interest rates to fight inflation, mainly in response to the strength of the US economy and the prospect of workers bidding up their wages.

Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies, said there was growing concern at the amount of debt being issued to fund government deficits, as well as inflation concerns.

“Inflation, deficit and issuance concerns continue to weigh on the bond market,” he said.

“There is also a buyers’ strike as investors do not want to step in till we get some form of stability. Hedge funds have suffered in the latest round of sell-off and do not have the risk appetite to fade the move. Real money potentially has the risk appetite, but won’t step in till we get some stability.”

Axel Rudolph, the chief technical analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “While the latest data has reduced expectations of an October Fed rate hike, investors remain wary that persistent inflation and higher oil prices could keep rates elevated for longer.

“The dollar is benefiting from that caution, climbing to a three-month high, while the prospect of a December rate increase keeps pressure on bond markets.”

Oil prices rose again on Thursday, despite analysis that showed exports of crude from the strait of Hormuz have largely returned to levels seen before the outbreak of the Iran war, as oil producers and the shipping industry have found alternative ways of transporting crucial fuel out of the Middle East.

Brent crude rose 3% to about $101 a barrel.

The price of crude remained at elevated levels as traders balanced the recovery in some Middle East exports with uncertainty over a long-term solution to the conflict and reopening of the strait.

Eurozone countries were also caught up in the wave of selling, with France in particular in investors’ sights. Ten-year yields on French government bonds hit 4.96%, the highest level since 2002.

The spread over German yields – an indicator of the additional risk France is believed to face – has jumped to its highest level in more than a decade.

FinanceTab.title: Federal Reserve watchdog finds no criminal violations for building renovation cost overruns
FinanceTab.text:
An internal watchdog said the Federal Reserve mismanaged costs associated with a $2.4bn renovation of its Washington DC headquarters, but noted that no criminal violations occurred, according to a report released on Wednesday.

For over a year, Donald Trump has centered his attacks against the Fed and former chair Jerome Powell around the renovations, including a months-long Department of Justice criminal investigation that was dropped in April.

The report said that the Fed’s board of governors “has not effectively managed” the construction project and “repeatedly deviated from its cost-management provisions”, but noted that the mismanagement was not criminal and that it did not find any administrative misconduct in its evaluation.

“At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred,” the report said.

Over the course of renovations, construction costs have gone from an initially budgeted $921m in February 2020 to $2.018bn by December 2024. Construction was supposed to be completed in mid-2024 but is not slated to go until December 2027.

The renovations have been a key part of the tension between the White House and the Fed, which by law is supposed to be non-partisan and independent. Trump has long been trying to pressure the Fed into lowering interest rates, to no avail.

Trump latched on to the Fed’s ongoing renovations as an attack point against Powell in June 2025, suggesting that it amounted to corruption. He suggested that renovations included elaborate features including a VIP dining room and a garden terrace.

In response, the Fed posted a video tour of the ongoing construction, noting that two buildings have not undergone renovations since the 1930s.

Trump visited the Fed’s headquarters to highlight the expenses that July. Donning hardhats in the bowels of the construction site, Trump and Powell had a spat over budget figures.

“It looks like it’s about $3.1bn,” Trump said at the time. “It went up a little bit or a lot.”

The typically reserved Powell became visibly annoyed. “I am not aware of that,” he said.

Soon after, Trump turned his Fed fight toward Fed governor Lisa Cook, whom he tried to fire over mortgage fraud. The supreme court ruled earlier this summer that the firing was unconstitutional because the White House did not follow proper procedure.

In January, Powell released a stunning video statement announcing that the Department of Justice was investigating the renovations as part of a criminal investigation, noting that the investigation was “pretext” for the Fed not lowering interest rates.

“This is about whether the Fed will be able to continue to set interest rates based on evidence and economic conditions – or whether instead monetary policy will be directed by political pressure or intimidation,” Powell said at the time.

The justice department investigation would end up stalling the confirmation of current Fed chair Kevin Warsh, after a key Republican senator said he would be a holdout until the department ended its investigation. In April, the justice department closed the investigation.

FinanceTab.title: Good news in US inflation report boosts chances Fed won’t hike rates
FinanceTab.text:
Good economic news boosted Wall Street’s main indexes on Wednesday, as a softer-than-anticipated inflation reading buoyed up hopes that the Federal Reserve might not hike rates as soon ⁠as next month.

A commerce department report ⁠showed the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) ​price index stood at 3.4% on an annual basis in August against estimates of 3.7%, per economists polled by Reuters.

Separately, second-quarter GDP data – the broadest measure of the economy’s health – showed that the US economy grew at a solid clip, driven ⁠by robust consumer spending and business investment related to the buildout of AI infrastructure.

“The market had been tracing out a bullish formation, meaning the price pattern suggested that any positive catalyst could trigger a move higher and that’s exactly ⁠what happened,” said Sam Stovall, chief investment strategist at CFRA Research.

Traders now see a roughly 35% chance of an October rate hike, down from about ​a 45% chance, according to data ‌compiled by LSEG. The Federal Reserve is under pressure to cut rates from the White House after raising them earlier this month for the first time since 2023.

Inflation has emerged as the top issue for voters in the run-up to the midterm elections with Donald Trump receiving poor marks for his handling of the economy.

US stock markets rose in early trading, but the S&P ended the day down 0.25% and the Dow fell 0.86%. The Nasdaq ended the day up 0.24%.

Despite weakness in September, driven by bond market volatility and elevated oil prices amid the US-Iran conflict, the benchmark S&P 500 and the ‌Nasdaq were on pace for a second straight quarterly advance, if gains hold.

On ​Wednesday, the yield on the 10-year treasury bond held steady at 5.246%, a day after hitting its highest since June 2007. Crude oil prices rose on the day, with the December contract for Brent crude futures moving higher.

There was also positive news from the jobs market. ADP, the US’s largest payroll supplier, said private employers added 90,000 jobs in September, higher than expected and up from 36,000 in August.

On Friday, the labor department will release its latest monthly jobs tally, which is expected to show a gain of 84,000 for September, down from 162,000 in the prior month.

Reuters contributed reporting

FinanceTab.title: A ‘freaked out’ US food industry is hitting back at Maha – with social media influencers
FinanceTab.text:
Some of the biggest food and agriculture corporations in the US are funding a campaign that pays social media influencers to combat elements of Robert F Kennedy Jr’s Make America Healthy Again platform, according to an investigation by the Guardian and Documented, an investigative watchdog and journalism project.

The ascension of RFK Jr to secretary of health and human services has boosted his putative campaign to end chronic illness in the US, which he believes is primarily caused by processed foods and dyes, exposure to certain chemicals, and poor farming practices, along with an overuse of what he falsely claims are dangerous vaccines. The “Maha” movement blends long-running mainstream concerns about food and farm safety with conspiracy theories about everything from medicine to milk. A Maha “summit” in Washington this week will feature JD Vance and several members of Trump’s cabinet.

A KFF poll from May 2026 reveals that some Maha themes resonate with a broad segment of US adults. About four in 10 say they support the Maha movement, while a majority of the public say there is not enough regulation of pesticides used in agriculture (64%) or of chemical food additives (75%).

Cross-partisan support in Washington on some of these issues poses a threat to the food industry’s bottom line – though the Trump administration has largely stopped short of enacting new regulations.

But several large corporations are fighting back. An effort by the Center for Food Integrity, an industry-funded non-profit, tracks public sentiment around key issues central to Maha and suggests ways that agricultural interests can counter those narratives by appealing to emotion or scientific reasoning.

They call it Gaha: Growing a Healthier America. Documents show the coordinated effort is tracking Maha closely and researching ways to respond to the movement’s claims without alienating its supporters. They are focused on several key areas: seed oils, pesticides, high-fructose corn syrup, regenerative agriculture, organic farming, raw milk/dairy and “big ag”, internal documents obtained by the Guardian and Documented show.

The campaign involves deploying social media influencers with significant reach online in an effort to rebuild trust in the industries that the Maha movement has made their target. The Gaha influencer campaign officially launched late last year. In February, CFI compiled a report listing dozens of sponsored posts on platforms such as online blogs, Facebook, TikTok and Instagram about key Gaha subjects. So far, at least six influencers have signed on to the Gaha campaign, reaching a total audience of more than 2.6 million viewers.

Influencers who participated in the paid campaign said they saw it as a way to counter misinformation that comes from Maha proponents, many of whom are paid to promote products in the wellness space. Some of the paid posts involved talking to farmers about pesticides or regenerative agriculture, which is the practice of restoring soil health, or explaining what seed oils are to counter claims that they cause a host of health problems.

In one July 2025 training video uncovered by the Guardian and Documented, the center explained the goal was to create an “echo chamber” among the food and agriculture industry groups, aligning them behind “the same ultimate message”.

“Without this coordinated response, that misinformation [from Maha] risks undermining consumer trust, fueling new regulations and eroding confidence in agriculture as a whole,” said Kelly Leighton, the center’s executive director, in the video.

The Center for Food Integrity, formed in 2007, conducts research and public relations campaigns on behalf of the food and agricultural sectors. The board consists of corporate executives from top brands: Bryan Malenius, CFI’s board president, also serves as the director of reputation strategy for public affairs at Chick-fil-A, while other members hold senior positions at companies such as Cargill, Dairy Farmers of America and the National Pork Board. Its members, whose dues pay to keep CFI operating, include groups such as the American Farm Bureau Federation and several state farm bureaus, CropLife America and the National Restaurant Association.

CFI created the Gaha campaign in partnership with its member organizations in the farming, agribusiness and food industries, in a bid to re-establish credibility with the public after Maha gained popularity. The American Farm Bureau Federation was also an important driver of the effort: the group’s president, Zippy Duvall, took credit for bringing industry groups together to form the Gaha coalition during a speech in January 2026.

Critiques of the food system, from pesticides to processed foods, have long been the purview of Democrats. With Maha, and Trump’s embrace of Robert F Kennedy Jr, the views have taken hold with many Republicans as well, presenting a broader threat to the agricultural industry.

“That surely freaks the industry out,” said Tom Philpott, senior research associate at the Center for a Livable Future at Johns Hopkins University. “For the industry, they are very concerned about, for want of a better word, a vibe shift.”

The Center for Food Integrity declined an interview request, saying in a statement: “At the Center for Food Integrity we recognize the critical link between diet and health. Growing a Healthier America supports an informed dialogue about how the food system can work together to assure a healthy affordable food supply and strong rural communities.”

The farm bureau also declined to comment, saying questions should be referred to CFI as it was their project.

Inside Gaha messaging

In mid-2025, the Gaha campaign began taking shape: CFI released a variety of resources for industry groups to use as a framework for their communications strategies moving forward.

The Guardian and Documented uncovered dozens of pages of internal materials related to this effort, including a “Say This, Not That” guide. It provided highly specific advice about language on key Maha topics, and included an influencer campaign creation guide.

Since last May, CFI has also released regular insight briefs, which identify Maha narratives gaining traction in the news and on social media, allowing industry to understand public sentiment shifts and adjust their messaging accordingly.

In a brief covering February and March, for example, the summary of online activity about processed foods noted that childhood obesity had reached a new high, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and cited a Canadian study linking ultra-processed foods in early childhood to “adverse behavioral and emotional changes” in children. On the following page, CFI pointed members to new resources to “support” their communications work specifically on the issue of processed foods.

CFI’s consumer research also directly informs who gets hired to deliver their messaging. An influencer campaign guide outlined preferred messengers for each consumer segment: for audiences who value authenticity, local farmers and wellness enthusiasts were best; for rationalists, scientists and dietitians; and for comfort seekers, CFI suggested lifestyle creators or faith-based voices.

Industry donors were invited to contribute hundreds of thousands of dollars to the Gaha campaign. An internal flyer revealed the perks for those who opt to contribute: supporters who pledge up to $50,000 receive regular updates, donors of up to $100,000 participate in quarterly meetings and provide strategic input, and contributors of more than $100,000 earn a seat on the leadership council, with the opportunity to review and approve strategy as well as help secure funding from others.

Why influencers got involved

According to a 12 August brief by the center, the campaign has had impact: Gaha has generated 13.2m impressions online, with more than 1.1m engagements and an 8.74% engagement rate.

Influencers who participated in the campaign posted about key topic areas the center wanted to target: raw milk, seed oils, agriculture. Some featured farmers talking about their work and how they balance using pesticides.

Slade Wentworth, who has more than 1 million followers on thedadbriefs, his Instagram account, said he participated in the campaign as part of a series he does that helps families “think critically through political and cultural noise”.

“In my opinion, many of the loudest voices in the Maha movement and in the food/wellness spaces in general tend to push anti- and pseudo-scientific claims,” Wentworth said via email. “To me, engaging with CFI was an opportunity to present a balanced discussion on topics that overlap with what I’d typically cover” in the series.

One of the topics he covered, on the raw milk movement, resonated well with his audience, he said. The comments he received on the work he did for the campaign were “varied and substantive”, a sign that the content “struck a good balance, enabling folks to lean into their perspectives thoughtfully”.

The anonymous creator of hydroxide.foodscience, which has more than 300,000 followers on Instagram, made posts about regenerative agriculture, ultra-processed foods and seed oils as part of the paid program. They decided to participate because it was a “uniquely positive spin on food and agriculture”.

“It can be difficult for people to sort through the weeds of food and food science and agriculture to really get the facts, so I think that was like a big reason why this campaign resonated with me,” they said. They do not disclose their name on their accounts.

Jessica Steier, the CEO of Unbiased Science, interviewed a farmer as part of the campaign to show what modern farming looks like. Unbiased Science received “a modest fee” for the campaign, but kept full editorial and scientific control, Steier said in an emailed statement. The center didn’t script the post or tell them what to say, which would have been a dealbreaker for Unbiased Science, she said. The work was not about defending industry, but about giving people information to make their own decisions, she said.

Much of the information amplified by Maha, Steier noted, falls under a “wave of chemophobia”, where people are told they’re being harmed without much evidence. Unbiased Science wanted to counter the fear by showing why farmers use pesticides, that the goal is to use the minimum amounts necessary and what regulations are in place, she said. Hearing it directly from a farmer “does something a fact sheet can’t”, she said.

“If anything, the financial incentives are far stronger on the other side of this,” Steier said. “The wellness economy that profits from fear about food and ‘toxins’ is enormously lucrative. Explaining why a preservative is safe is not where the money is. The people being richly rewarded for shaping what Americans believe about their food are not the ones defending the evidence.”

Other influencers the center included in its campaign were Happy Strong Healthy, Dietitian Hannah and Veggies and Chocolate. These accounts did not respond to emailed requests for comment.

Maha as ‘existential threat’

Jerold Mande, a nutritionist who served as deputy undersecretary for food safety at the US Department of Agriculture under Barack Obama, said the campaign sounds like “crisis management”. He has worked for decades to make food policy a priority, but thinks Maha, with its cross-partisan appeal, represents the biggest threat to the food industry that he’s seen. Using influencers to counter Maha, which is in essence a loose grouping of influencers itself, makes sense.

“They realize now that they’re facing an existential threat, and their whole business model over the last decades has evolved around, you know, how do we make money?” Mande said.

Still, he said, as Maha has charted some wins and made food policy a political priority, it has failed to install regulations that would create meaningful changes.

“You’re not going to make progress if you don’t use government’s two powerful levers: funding and rules,” Mande said.

Marion Nestle, a molecular biologist and nutritionist who has studied and written about food politics, said food and agriculture groups are always working to protect their industries, so a campaign like this is “nothing new”, especially when Republicans are now talking about agrochemicals. “Of course, they’re going to lobby, and they’re going to do it in absolutely every way they can,” Nestle said.

Using an outright attack on Maha influencers, many of whom are moms whom Nestle believes “really care about their kids”, would not be a good idea, she said, leading to softer and more behind-the-scenes methods to sway opinion.

Maha isn’t “getting anywhere” with major changes to the food system, given the refusal to regulate coming from Kennedy and the Trump administration, she said.

“Food companies have license to do all the lobbying they want, and they can say whatever they want,” she said. “They don’t have to do anything. Nobody’s making them do anything. Nobody’s holding them accountable for anything.”

This article was produced in partnership with Documented, an investigative watchdog and journalism project. Riley Messer is a senior researcher at Documented.

FinanceTab.title: US ban on Canadian imports likely to weaken already fragile relationship
FinanceTab.text:
US-Canada relations, already tense, are likely to deteriorate further after the United States went ahead early on Tuesday with a decision to ban nearly $1bn worth of Canadian imports, including alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles.

The ban amounts to barely a ripple in $880bn worth of annual two-way trade between the two northern neighbors. But it marks another ratcheting up of Donald Trump’s second-term trade war with the US’s longtime ally and trading partner.

The import ban “certainly won’t do anything to help the trade tensions between the United States and Canada’,’ said trade attorney Patrick Childress, a partner at Holland + Knight and a former US trade official.

The latest sparring began over the summer when Trump reached back to a Great Depression law to impose 50% tariffs on about $20bn worth of Canadian imports, charging that Canada discriminates against US dairy, auto and alcoholic beverage producers. Canada promptly counterpunched with tariffs of 15%, 25% or 50%, matching US imports dollar for dollar.

To punish Canada for retaliating against his tariffs, Trump decided to ban a list of Canadian products, effective 12.01 am Eastern time Tuesday.

The economic impact is likely to be minimal. Childress noted that the products on the banned list were already facing Trump’s tariffs. “For a lot of these goods, the 50% was already acting as a de facto ban by making importation from Canada into the United States uneconomical,″ he said.

Jacob Jensen, director of trade policy at the center-right American Action Forum thinktank, calculates that the ban would cover $967m worth of Canadian imports, based on 2025 numbers. Of that, 87% would be alcoholic beverages that the US targeted because of some Canadian provinces responding to Trump’s provocations by banning US booze from store shelves.

Also banned are some dairy products – including the milk byproduct whey. The two countries have long clashed over Canada’s attempts to protect its dairy industry from foreign competition by imposing hefty tariffs once dairy imports have exceeded a quota.

The ban also covers motorcycles. Bombardier Recreational Products (BRP) in Quebec confirmed that its three-wheel Can-Am Spyder and Canyon motorcycles “will be excluded from importation into the US’’. But BRP said the impact would probably not be felt until next year because it has completed most production and shipments for the current season.

“This marks yet another escalation in the trade war that may result in further retaliation on the Canadian side,” Jensen said. He expects Canadian exporters and US importers “impacted by these bans will be highly motivated’’ to demand that trade officials on both sides find some way to reach a “resolution of this whole ordeal’’.

The impasse imperils efforts to renew the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, a North American trade pact Trump pressured the US’s neighbors into accepting in his first term and which he once declared “the most modern, up-to-date, and balanced trade agreement in the history of our country’’.

The deal allowed most goods to cross North American borders duty free. But since returning to the White House last year, Trump has announced a series of tariffs that have clouded the future of trade in the region.

Trump has directed most of his ire at Canada. He is openly seeking to pull Canadian manufacturing south. And he has inflamed public opinion in Canada by repeatedly suggesting that the country become the US’s 51st state.

The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, came to power last year on a promise to stand up to Trump. In addition to retaliating against Trump tariffs, Carney has sought to reduce Canada’s reliance on the United States, which last year accounted for more than 70% of Canadian exports.

“There is now a price to be paid for access to the United States market,” Carney said earlier this month. Carney has embraced the prospect of Canada becoming the European Union’s first associate member.

SportsTab.title: Man City: HMRC urged to scrutinise tax implications of verdict revealed by Premier League
SportsTab.text:
Findings from the Premier League's case against Manchester City require scrutiny from His Majesty's Revenue and Customs, the chair of a cross-party group of MPs has told the tax authority.

It was confirmed on Tuesday that an independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

City have repeatedly denied guilt, and have signalled an intent to lodge an appeal by Friday.

The club were found to have artificially inflated revenue through "sham" sponsorship agreements with the help of their owners.

The independent commission which studied the case found City "utilised devices" to "disguise the true extent of certain club liabilities".

The Treasury Committee, which is responsible for overseeing policies and administration of HMRC, has therefore asked whether the government department has requested the redacted documents contained within the commission's report.

Dame Meg Hillier, chair of the Treasury Committee, said she would "welcome reassurance from HMRC that you are seized of the importance of these issues and the public interest in this case".

Manchester City, who deny wrongdoing, will claim as part of their appeal that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners.

Owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy prime minister Sheikh Mansour - are said to have topped up the value of commercial deals as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to the scale of £830.69m.

This, it was argued, enabled the club to appear to comply with Premier League and Uefa financial rules.

However, as first reported by the Daily Mail and Times, sources have told BBC Sport that City are expected to tell an appeal board that they have evidence showing the money directed to sponsors came from the Abu Dhabi government, rather than from ADUG.

The independent commission rejected this argument as "untrue" in its findings, saying: "We concluded that it was an 'explanation' that the club had concocted well after the event in an attempt to obscure and conceal the realities of the disguised funding scheme."

City have claimed the commission's decision contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe".

Mansour is a member of the ruling family of Abu Dhabi, and the brother of UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. ADUG took over City in 2008. Premier League rules allow state-owned bodies to sponsor clubs.

On Saturday, City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak referred to "irrefutable evidence" that he claimed supports the club's claims of innocence.

City's principal sponsor Etihad Airways has said it is considering legal action against the Premier League, claiming the release of the commission findings had "damaging implications… despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings".

The UAE's state-owned national airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements".

Etihad is owned by sovereign wealth fund L'Imad which is chaired by the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, the son of the UAE president.

The Premier League declined to comment when contacted by BBC Sport.

SportsTab.title: Man City not 'above the rules', says No 10 after backlash to Burnham remarks
SportsTab.text:
Downing Street has said Manchester City are not "above the rules" after Andy Burnham was criticised for his comments about the club's breaches of Premier League financial rules.

The prime minister said on Wednesday he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners decide to sell up after City were found guilty by an independent commission of most of the 115 charges they faced.

His remarks were branded "completely out of touch" and "extraordinary" by the Tories and took many in the football community by surprise.

In a statement following the backlash, Downing Street said the PM had made clear "the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules".

In an attempt to clarify the PM's position, a No 10 spokesperson added: "He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected.

"Wherever wrondoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."

Man City deny any wrongdoing and have until Friday to submit an appeal.

Sources told BBC Sport that City are expected to claim that key sponsorship deals were funded by the Abu Dhabi government, rather than the club's owners, as part of an appeal.

Among the independent panel's findings were that City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.

The Premier League said City "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade".

In an interview on Wednesday with the BBC's political editor Chris Mason, Burnham - who was mayor of Greater Manchester until June - said he was "not getting directly involved in the process", saying it must be undertaken independently by the Premier League.

He said the situation was "contested by Manchester City" and it would be "wrong" to "jump to a conclusion".

Asked if he was worried the club's owners since 2008 - led by Sheikh Mansour, a royal and the United Arab Emirates deputy prime minister - might sell up, Burnham said: "I would be really concerned to lose them.

"They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.

"I can't intervene more in the process, it would be wrong for me to do that."

In response, the Tories accused Burnham of "publicly backing the owners even as the investigation continues" and questioned whether "political pressure" was being applied.

SportsTab.title: David Beckham, Harry Kane, Gareth Bale: Ranking the best British exports this century
SportsTab.text:
Gazza's baggy Roman shellsuit, John Charles plundering black-and-white goals in Turin, King Kev's floodlit perm dazzling Volksparkstadion terraces, Glenn Hoddle's minuscule Monegasque shorts.

They were all trailblazers and trendsetters, their tales relayed through continental dispatches and espresso-fuelled Saturday morning showreels.

Yet what was once an exotic European escapade for Britain's star footballers is now a well-trodden pilgrimage, as an increasing number of players eye opportunities further afield.

Eight of England's most recent World Cup squad are currently playing abroad - from Munich to Madrid, and Milan to the Middle East - while Scotland have even more overseas, predominantly in Serie A.

So while we acknowledge and applaud the groundwork put in by those early jetsetters, this week we're looking at the best British exports since the turn of the century.

I've ranked my top 10 below - you can have you say in the comments, too.

10. Kieran Trippier - Atletico Madrid

Kieran Trippier was seemingly deemed surplus to requirements at Tottenham after the north London outfit's Champions League final defeat by Liverpool in 2019, but the defender managed to renew his career under Diego Simeone in Spain.

The right-back became Atletico Madrid's first English player in almost a century, and then helped Los Rojiblancos win only their second La Liga title since the turn of the millennium, breaking the Barcelona and Real Madrid stranglehold.

It was the first trophy of his career, and Trippier returned to the Premier League after his Spanish sabbatical renewed, refreshed and ready to enjoy a successful spell at Newcastle.

9. Fikayo Tomori - AC Milan

John Charles, three-times winner; Jimmy Greaves, with Milan in 1961-62; and Gerry Hitchens, with Inter the following season, were the only British players to clinch a Scudetto before Juventus' Aaron Ramsey ended a wait that stretched back more than half a century in 2020.

Ramsey's Turin expedition, though, was inconsistent and expensive, and while Ashley Young then helped Inter win a first title in 11 years, his San Siro stay lasted only 18 months.

So the Scudetto winner we're plumping for here is Milan stalwart Fikayo Tomori.

The England defender lifted the prize in 2021-22, earning a spot in the Serie A team of the season on the way. And, despite ups and downs under various bosses since, the 28-year-old is now into his seventh season with the European giants. A quietly impressive feat.

8. Jadon Sancho - Borussia Dortmund

Jadon Sancho's career may not have continued on the trajectory many expected when he departed Germany in a £73m move for Old Trafford, four years after initially leaving Manchester, but his time at Dortmund was an undoubted success.

It was brave, as a 17-year-old, to reject Manchester City and move to a new country, but the young winger was vindicated with rapid progress at Dortmund.

In his second season, Sancho scored 12 goals and added 18 assists in 34 Bundesliga games, the following term he netted 17 times.

In fact, by the time Sancho left Dortmund aged 21 he'd scored 50 goals and made 64 assists across 137 games in all competitions, winning a German Cup and finishing runner-up in both the European Golden Boy prize and the Kopa Trophy for the world's best young player.

More than that, he helped establish a pathway for young British prospects to grow and develop abroad that many have followed since.

7. David Beckham - Real Madrid, LA Galaxy, AC Milan & PSG

It was tempting to include Bradley Wright-Philips, a man who followed a half-season stint at League One Brentford with a move to New York Red Bulls, winning a pair of Golden Boots, three Supporters' Shields and netting more than 100 goals during his time in the Big Apple.

But if we're talking Major League Soccer impact then there's only one winner. David Beckham swapped the Galactico comforts of Real Madrid, where he spent four seasons and collected a sole La Liga crown, for a Hollywood welcome at LA Galaxy.

Beckham's presence was at times questioned, especially when spending loan spells in Milan, but the England captain and global superstar brought a huge amount of eyeballs and allure to the American game. He left with silverware, too, twice winning both the MLS Cup and Supporters' Shield.

There was room for a five-month stay in Paris before the midfielder hung up his iconic Preds, winning Ligue 1 and waving an emotional goodbye in 2013.

6. Scott McTominay - Napoli

Maybe it's the tomatoes. Scott McTominay wouldn't touch one back in Manchester, but since moving to southern Italy he boasts the glow of a man loving both the local Neapolitan cuisine and his football.

The Lancaster-born Scot has undergone a slick transformation. Few would have expected him to veer from United squad player to cult hero mentioned in the same breath as Napoli's greatest adopted son, Diego Maradona.

But McTominay, with a little help from compatriot Billy Gilmour, has thrived in the football-obsessed maze that is Naples, firing the club to only a fourth Scudetto in history with 12 goals from midfield during his debut Serie A season.

It landed him the league's MVP award.

Finishing runners-up last term, McTominay has already etched his name in Napoli folklore, with more goals - and tomatoes - likely to follow.

5. Owen Hargreaves - Bayern Munich

Owen Hargreaves is something of an anomaly. You could argue he shouldn't count as an export given he was born and raised in Canada, before moving to Bayern Munich aged 16.

Indeed, he's the only player to represent England without having previously lived there. But winning 42 Three Lions caps legitimises his inclusion.

Born in Calgary, having also represented Wales at youth level, Hargreaves cleaned up on the silverware front during his seven seasons in Munich - winning four Bundesliga titles and several German Cups.

Yet his most impressive achievement came in Europe.

Then a 20-year-old, yet to be capped by England, he played 120 minutes in central midfield alongside captain Stefan Effenberg as Bayern beat Valencia on penalties at San Siro in 2001.

Several British players previously lost European Cup finals for foreign clubs - Kevin Keegan with Hamburg, Laurie Cunningham at Real Madrid, Steve Archibald with Barcelona and Chris Waddle at Marseille.

But Hargreaves became only the third to win it - and only two have done so since. Dortmund's Paul Lambert in 1997 was the first, we'll get to the others in a moment.

2. Steve McManaman - Real Madrid

Was Steve McManaman underappreciated? He perhaps didn't earn the number of England caps his talent deserved. In fact, the last of those 37 Three Lions outings came before he won a second Champions League with Real Madrid, despite pleas from club team-mates such as Zinedine Zidane that he should be given a recall.

The marauding winger's move to Madrid in the summer of 1999 was unique - he was the first English player since Laurie Cunningham in 1982 to feature for Los Merengues and the first to move to the Bernabeu directly from the Premier League.

It came at a time when Spanish football was harder to consume for UK audiences, before the peak Revista de la Liga era, making McManaman, renowned for his dribbling and creativity, something of an enigma.

But the Bootle-born player enjoyed an impressive four-season stint in Spain, scoring a volley against Valencia in the Champions League final win of 2000 and coming off the bench to collect another winner's medal two years later, adding to two La Liga successes.

1. Gareth Bale - Real Madrid & LAFC

There is, however, one clear leader when it comes to the best British exports since the turn of the century - and potentially of all time.

Gareth Bale, the Welsh marvel, has more Champions League winner's medals than the rest of this list combined. He has five of them, in fact, which came across a nine-year spell when Real Madrid dominated Europe's showpiece competition.

Bale's commitment to Los Blancos' cause was sometimes questioned - he once held up a flag that claimed Wales, and golf, were his priorities - but his return was still impressive and he insisted he always gave his all for Real.

The flying forward scored 106 goals in 258 games, with three of those coming in Champions League finals, including an outrageous overhead kick in 2018.

His short stint before retirement in Los Angeles was less memorable, but still yielded a Supporters' Shield and MLS Cup triumph, where he scored a last-gasp leveller before LAFC won on penalties.

SportsTab.title: 2027 Cricket World Cup draw: England avoid Australia & India in group stage
SportsTab.text:
England have avoided defending champions Australia and world number one-ranked side India in the group-stage draw for the 2027 ICC Men's Cricket World Cup.

India and Pakistan are, once again, placed in the same group, alongside Australia, Afghanistan, Zimbabwe and a qualifier.

England, who won the trophy in 2019, are in the same group as co-hosts South Africa, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, New Zealand and a qualifier.

Harry Brook's side, who have enjoyed a resurgence in the 50-over format, begin their campaign against Bangladesh on 8 October, and Sri Lanka on 13 October in Windhoek, Namibia.

They will come up against South Africa in Gqeberha on 16 October before travelling to Harare to face a qualifier on 20 October. They round off the group stage when they face New Zealand, again in Gqeberha, on 23 October.

The visit to Zimbabwe is significant, with England having not played there since 2004.

Political unrest in Zimbabwe under the regime of former president Robert Mugabe caused problems for England's men's team throughout the 2000s.

England boycotted their fixture against Zimbabwe in Harare at the 2003 World Cup - a decision which ultimately derailed their campaign.

Relations have improved in recent years, however, and BBC Sport reported in 2025 that the two cricket boards were discussing a potential England tour of the country in the next cycle of international cricket between 2027 and 2031.

After three matches to decide the final two qualifiers, the tournament group stage will open with a repeat of the 2023 final when India and Australia face each other in Cape Town on 7 October.

Arch-rivals India and Pakistan, who do not play each other outside tournaments, will meet in Johannesburg on 10 October.

The top three, plus the best fourth-placed finisher, from the two groups progress to the Super 7 stage.

From there, the top four teams will qualify for the semi-finals, which are scheduled for 17 and 18 November, before the final on 21 November in Johannesburg.

SportsTab.title: Sporting scandals that shook the world: Lance Armstrong, Hansie Cronje, 'Crashgate'
SportsTab.text:
Manchester City being found guilty of fuelling an era of glittering Premier League success via a network of sponsorship deals, found by an independent commission to be a "sham", has shaken the world of sport.

But it isn't the first time.

The lure of glory and riches on the biggest stages have tempted plenty of others to cheat.

BBC Sport looks back on nine more sporting scandals, stretching back more than a century.

Cancer survivor. Cycling legend. American hero. Cheat.

Lance Armstrong had spent years vehemently and aggressively insisting that he had won all seven of his Tour de France titles between 1999 and 2005 without the help of performance-enhancing drugs.

His story was remarkable. Aged 25, Armstrong had been diagnosed with testicular cancer, with doctors warning he was likely to die given the disease had spread to other parts of his body.

He not only survived, but returned to dominate top-level cycling. His Livestrong Foundation was wildly successful, selling millions of yellow wristbands to raise money to support fellow cancer sufferers.

However, as the evidence and former team-mates allegations against him stacked up, Armstrong was stripped of his Tour de France titles.

Armstong eventually confessed to cheating in a blockbuster interview with talk show host Oprah Winfrey.

"I made those decisions, they were my mistake and I'm here to say sorry," he said, adding that the culture in professional cycling made using drugs non-negotiable.

Hansie Cronje was the golden boy of South African sport.

Good looking and charming, he led the nation's cricket team with style and authority.

President Nelson Mandela singled out Cronje in 1996 for the "excellent manner" in which he captained the Proteas.

However, Cronje's love of money, combined with a fast-growing betting industry and the organised crime it attracted, proved his downfall.

Cronje entertained the offers of match-fixers, calling team meetings to discuss the possibility of throwing matches and sharing thousands of dollars in inducements.

Most infamously, Cronje contrived to lose a rain-affected Test against England in 2000.

With South Africa still in the midst of their first innings on the final day, Cronje convinced England counterpart Nasser Hussain that in the interest of sporting entertainment each side should forfeit an innings, producing a sudden run-chase and giving England a shot at victory.

Cronje was praised for his Corinthian spirit. In reality, he had been motivated by a bribe of £5,000 to ensure the match did not end in a draw.

Cronje was undone when an Indian police wiretap of a bookmaker caught him in discussions about fixing matches.

Cronje confessed in early 2000, was banned from cricket for life and died in a plane crash two years later at the age of 32.

There was something particular about turn 17 of the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

In 2008, before the inaugural Singapore Grand Prix was held at the circuit, Renault driver Nelson Piquet Jr knew it did not have any overhead cranes to lift a damaged car from the track. There were no side entrances to allow a stranded driver to be pushed out of danger's way by marshals either.

On lap 14, Piquet Jr found himself in exactly in that unfortunate position. And, despite his initial claim that he had made a "simple mistake", the Brazilian had put himself there deliberately.

When Renault dropped him in 2009, Piquet Jr revealed that he steered himself into a concrete wall to crash his car. The safety car was deployed as officials cleared debris off the track.

Crucially, Piquet Jr's team-mate Fernando Alonso was the only frontrunner to have stopped for fuel and new tyres at the point of the crash.

As Alonso's rivals went into the pits, the Spaniard, benefiting from the reduced gaps caused by the safety car, moved up the field and went on to win the race.

While Alonso was cleared of any wrongdoing or knowledge of the plot, Renault team principal Flavio Briatore and chief technical officer Pat Symonds were banned from F1 for several years.

Frank Lampard wheeled away in celebration after his well-hit shot from the edge of the penalty area beat Kevin Miller in the Crystal Palace goal in the 65th minute of a Monday evening Premier League game in November 1997.

As he was mobbed by team-mates, Upton Park was plunged into darkness.

The following month similar happened at Selhurst Park. Thirteen seconds into the second half - with Wimbledon and Arsenal goalless - the lights went off. The Christmas lights in nearby Croydon were raised as a possible cause.

The actual cause was more sinister.

An Asian betting syndicate had pulled the plug, using a remote control circuit breaker, to get each match abandoned at a scoreline which would maximise their profits.

The gang were foiled in their attempts to pull the deception for a third time. They had bribed a security guard at Charlton Athletic to allow them to plant a device at The Valley before Liverpool's visit in February.

However, a suspicious member of staff at the club tipped off police.

Four men were given sentences of between 18 months and four years for their involvement.

No expense was spared for the Winter Olympics in Sochi in 2014.

With a budget of $50bn (£38bn) - more than 25 times Vancouver's 2010 Winter Olympics spend - organisers created two entirely new resorts, bristling with security and military personnel.

But building facilities from scratch also gave the Russian hosts a chance to design an elaborate way around anti-doping measures.

A secret tunnel allowed a Russian secret service agent, disguised as a sewer engineer, to swap out his compatriots' urine samples, which contained traces of banned substances.

A special method had been developed to remove the tamper-proof lids of sample bottles, which were then refilled with 'clean' urine that had been frozen before Russian athletes began doping programmes.

Forty-three Russian athletes were banned for life, 28 of whom successfully appealed against the full extent of their punishment.

Russia was banned from competing at the following Winter Olympics in South Korea, although athletes who could demonstrate a clean record were permitted to compete under a neutral flag.

A camera crew caught the aftermath of the attack on Nancy Kerrigan in January 1994.

The 24-year-old figure skater was captured clutching her leg and repeatedly wailing "why?".

Kerrigan had been training at a rink in Detroit before the American national championships. As she stepped off the ice, a man rushed towards her and struck her on the leg with a telescopic baton.

Kerrigan's 'why' was soon answered.

The bodyguard and ex-husband of Kerrigan's rival Tonya Harding had hired a man to break Kerrigan's leg. They hoped to rule her out of the forthcoming Winter Olympics in Lillehammer, boosting Harding's chances.

It didn't work. Kerrigan recovered from heavy bruising in time to make the USA team, alongside Harding.

Amid a media frenzy, Harding, struggling with a broken lace on her boot, finished eighth in the Olympic final.

Kerrigan took silver.

The competition broke viewing records in the US.

Harding was banned for life from the sport after admitting attempting to conceal the identity of Kerrigan's assailant after the attack.

Harding's ex-husband Jeff Gillooly, the attacker he hired, and a getaway driver, all spent time in prison for their part in the crime.

"Say it ain't so Joe."

The headline written in the Chicago Daily News summed up the disbelief of a city, a nation and a sport when it emerged that superstar Joe Jackson and seven of his Chicago White Sox team-mates had apparently taken bribes to lose the 1919 World Series, baseball's biggest game.

First baseman Chick Gandil was the ringleader, while star pitcher Eddie Cicotte was the key figure.

A fee of $100,000 - worth about $1.6m today - was agreed with the head of a betting syndicate, with the money to be shared among the eight conspirators.

Cicotte's pitch, deliberately hitting Maurice Rath on the back, was a sign to his team-mates, and gamblers in the know, that the fix was on.

After the White Sox lost the series 5-3 to the Cincinnati Reds, the White Sox's suspicious owner Charles Comiskey sent word that the players needed to collect their pay cheques from him in person.

None of the eight fixers did. They left the stadium without their money. Rumours spread, followed by an investigation, and soon the players were in the dock.

Although a criminal court failed to convict the players, they were banned from Major League Baseball for life.

Jackson insisted until his death in 1951 that he was not involved and that, despite receiving $5,000, he had been deceived into signing a confession.

At half-time in their first match at the 2000 Paralympics the coach of Spain's intellectual disability basketball team told them to stop scoring so quickly and let their opponents shoot more.

He knew the vast majority of the team were there under false pretences.

Of the 12 players in the squad, 10 had no intellectual impairment at all but were keen amateur players who had been recruited months before the Sydney Games to supplement the team.

Spain, perhaps unsurprisingly, won gold convincingly, beating Russia 87-63 in the final.

The scam unravelled because one of the ringers was also a journalist.

Realising he was in the midst of an incredible scoop, Carlos Ribagorda played in Sydney and then published an article detailing the scandal on his return.

The team were stripped of their medals and the incident led to a total ban on athletes with an intellectual disability from the 2004 and 2008 Paralympics, destroying the careers of thousands of sportspeople around the world.

When public prosecutors tapped telephone calls at Italian football giants Juventus in 2004, they were hunting for evidence of doping.

What they believed they found was corruption on a far more systematic scale.

They thought they had evidence of Juve general manager Luciano Moggi pressurising referee officials to favour certain clubs, including his own. Moggi denied the claims.

However, Juve, AC Milan, Fiorentina, Lazio and Reggina were all implicated in influencing referees.

All were given points deductions, but only Juventus ultimately dropped into the second tier of Italian football.

There was a split in the club's superstar squad.

Zlatan Ibrahimovic and Patrick Vieira joined rivals Inter Milan for a combined £23m, Fabio Cannavaro and Emerson went to Real Madrid for £13.7m, Lilian Thuram and Gianluca Zambrotta joined Barcelona for £13m, and Adrian Mutu went to Fiorentina for £5.5m.

But other key players – notably Gianluigi Buffon, Alessandro del Piero, Giorgio Chiellini, Pavel Nedved and David Trezeguet – remained with Juve in Serie B.

Despite beginning the season with a nine-point penalty and an opening-day draw with minnows Rimini, Juventus were promoted at the first attempt.

The club still lay claim to the 2004–05 and 2005–06 titles that were stripped from them, counting 38 rather than the official 36.

SportsTab.title: Arsenal: Was penalty after Leah Williamson handball the correct decision in Champions League?
SportsTab.text:
A bizarre error from Arsenal defender Leah Williamson proved costly in their 2-2 draw with Paris FC on Wednesday in the Women's Champions League.

With the Gunners leading 2-1 late on, England captain Williamson stopped a short goal-kick with her hand - believing it had not been taken and that she was to take it - resulting in a penalty being awarded to the hosts, converted by Maeline Mendy.

The unusual incident means the Gunners are fourth in the Champions League table after their opening two games, but would have been second with a victory in the French capital.

After the ball had gone out of play for a goal-kick, Arsenal goalkeeper Misa Rodriguez played a quick, short pass to Williamson.

Williamson had her arm stretched out to stop the ball and place it so that she could take the goal-kick herself.

With the ball being still and on the field of play when Rodriguez played the ball to Williamson, that was deemed to be the goal-kick instead of Williamson's attempt.

Therefore Williamson was penalised for handball and Mendy levelled the match from the penalty spot.

While Arsenal felt aggrieved at the decision, the guidance on such incidents state that the decision to award a penalty was correct.

Guidance from Law 16 of the International Football Association Board's (Ifab) laws of the game state: "In goal-kick restarts, if the ball is stationary within the goal area and is kicked by any defending player, the goal-kick is considered to have been taken.

"If, after the ball is in play, [a player] commits a handball offence, a penalty kick is awarded if the offence occurred inside the kicker's penalty area.

Law 12 from Ifab also states: "It is an offence if a player deliberately touches the ball with their hand/arm."

In November 2024, Aston Villa defender Tyrone Mings committed an identical error in a Champions League match against Club Brugge.

Brugge won a penalty that was scored by Hans Vanaken, with the Belgian side winning the match 1-0.

"The biggest mistake I witnessed in my career," said Villa boss Unai Emery at the time.

Earlier that year, Gunners centre-back Gabriel also made the mistake in a Champions League match against Bayern Munich.

However in that instance, Arsenal were given the chance to retake the goal-kick.

"He [Gabriel] touched the ball with the hand because he thought it was not in game, but it was in game and the referee admitted it was in game and was handball," said then Bayern boss Thomas Tuchel.

The now England head coach also said that the error in not awarding Bayern a penalty was a "kid's mistake".

Arsenal's assistant coach Aaron D'Antino conducted post-match media duties and explained that, while the intention was for Williamson to take the goal-kick, they will use the incident as a learning experience.

"If we're looking at what we can control, it's just passing the ball to Leah from what I remember seeing. The ball was still rolling and she [Rodriguez] was moving it to Leah for her to take the goal-kicks as we normally do," said D'Antino.

"So maybe the learning in that is how we get the ball to Leah, so we don't put ourselves in that situation."

Former Arsenal and Scotland defender Jen Beattie felt the referee Iuliana Demetrescu got the decision wrong, despite the correct applications of the laws.

"For me, I just don't even know how that happens. Leah knows it's a goal-kick, she's catching the ball. That's shocking from the referee," Beattie told Paramount+.

"I would have been fuming and I would have been embarrassed if they gave that. This is not what they're trying to do. It's just beyond frustrating that that's how they've tied the game.

"Leah's obviously going [to do that] because she's going to take the goal-kick, not because she's worried about the press or trying to change it - or panicking in any situation. Leah Williamson doesn't panic in those moments, she knows what she's doing. The goalkeeper knows what she's doing as well.

"The referee has miscalled it."

This article is the latest from BBC Sport's Ask Me Anything team.

SportsTab.title: England cricket news: Crane called up and Archer rested for Pakistan tri-series
SportsTab.text:
Leg-spinner Mason Crane could play for England for the first time in eight years after being recalled for the one-day international tri-series in Pakistan.

The 29-year-old won his only Test cap against Australia in Sydney in 2018 and is now given an opportunity in the series which also involves Sri Lanka next month.

Crane, who also played two T20 internationals in 2017, could also push his case in the fight to be England's number one spinner in Test cricket.

Sam Curran and Adil Rashid both return after injuries, and uncapped pair James Coles and Henry Crocombe are included.

Jos Buttler is out with the hamstring injury he sustained last week, while Jacob Bethell is continuing his recovery from knee surgery.

Brydon Carse, who is under an investigation from the Cricket Regulator following an incident outside a nightclub in Derby in August, remains absent.

———————————————————

England squad for tri-series in Pakistan: Harry Brook (Yorkshire – captain), Gus Atkinson (Surrey), Sonny Baker (Hampshire), Tom Banton (Somerset), James Coles (Sussex), Jordan Cox (Essex), Mason Crane (Glamorgan), Henry Crocombe (Sussex), Sam Curran (Surrey), Liam Dawson (Hampshire), Ben Duckett (Nottinghamshire), Will Jacks (Surrey), Jamie Overton (Surrey), Adil Rashid (Yorkshire), Joe Root (Yorkshire), Josh Tongue (Nottinghamshire).

———————————————————

England are on a diet of white-ball cricket until three Tests in South Africa in December as they build up to the 50-over World Cup in southern Africa next year.

The tri-series in Pakistan involves the three teams taking part playing each other twice, with the top two advancing to the final. Following the trip to Pakistan, England play three one-day internationals and five T20s in Australia in November.

As England continue to shape their backroom staff following the arrival of Stephen Fleming as Test coach, Jeetan Patel, Mike Yardy, David Saker and Carl Hopkinson will assist white-ball head coach Brendon McCullum in Pakistan.

That means Marcus Trescothick, who took temporary charge of the Test team for the series against Pakistan in the home summer, misses the trip.

It is understood the make-up of the coaching staff is part of a plan to rotate the coaches – fielding coach Sarah Taylor and fast-bowling coach Tim Southee are also not going to Pakistan.

All of Trescothick, Taylor and Southee are likely to be part of England's coaching team for other tours this winter.

SportsTab.title: Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia: George Russell on confidence
SportsTab.text:
George Russell says he "doesn't feel lost any more" as he seeks to end a difficult season on a high and chase down team-mate Kimi Antonelli's championship lead.

Russell won his third race of the season in Azerbaijan last weekend, and his first for three months, and says he has made a breakthrough in terms of understanding how to drive the Mercedes car.

The Briton trails Antonelli by 66 points in the championship with either seven or eight races still remaining.

"The thing that's changed is I feel my performances are strong enough to fight for victory week in week out," Russell said.

"I know what I need from the car and myself and I don't really feel lost any more.

"Confidence is back and it's growing again and it's all coming a bit more naturally, which is how it has been for most of my career and not how it's been for most of the season."

Mercedes are expecting a strong challenge from McLaren at the flowing Sepang track this weekend as its characteristics should suit the world champions' car.

But the team have their first major upgrade for some time and hope that will bring them into contention.

Asked whether another strong performance at this weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia could change the psychology of the title fight, Russell said: "I've never really felt in a position to fight for the victories because my performances weren't strong enough.

"But now finally I feel I'm in a place I can fight for victory week in week out.

"Of course there is a big deficit in the championship, but there is a third of a season to go and still so much can happen. I am just going to go race by race. I feel more at one with the car and hopefully this upgrade will play into my favour a bit more. So bring it on."

Russell started the season as championship favourite but Antonelli took control early on as Russell struggled to get to grips with the Mercedes designed for this year's all-new car and engine rules.

He has had to "consciously adjust" his driving style.

"I went through a few races where I was having to think how to make those adjustments, whereas now it's all just a bit more intuitive and a bit more natural," Russell said.

"So what I set out to achieve, in terms of getting the car [into] a slightly better window, I'm now achieving without having to think about it as much. So I can just focus on driving fast."

Antonelli had a difficult weekend in Baku, with a crash in qualifying leaving him 16th on the grid, from where he recovered to finished fifth.

The Italian said: "Last weekend was probably there worst weekend from me of the season.

"But still good learning from the weekend and was also a very strange race for me in Baku because it was one of those races where I consciously tried not to take any risks and just drive under the limit which was very weird but it was what I needed on Sunday. I needed a clean result after a very disrupted weekend.

"I wasn't happy after the race but I learned the most important learning was I need to be always 100% because if I don't try to do everything right in my power then nothing is going to come my way."

Lewis Hamilton has declared Frederic Vasseur as "the guy to lead us" two days after Ferrari made an unusual public statement backing their team principal after speculation over this position.

The seven-time champion, who is third in the drivers' title race while Ferrari are second in the constructors' battle, said removing Vasseur would be a mistake.

"He's doing a fantastic job," Hamilton said. If you look at the history, how many people [have been swapped] out [of] that role… and I feel like it's in a better place than it's been before.

"But it's not a one-man situation. It's lots and lots of people coming together and if you want to point fingers, point it somewhere else. There's people above who are also part of it.

"Fred's in his position, he's not going anywhere and I'm here to stay with him and I still believe fully in where we're going.

"Swapping him out won't change how the team is moving forward. If anything it will be detrimental."

Hamilton pointed to the progress Ferrari have made since a winless 2025 season, in which they finished fourth in the teams' championship. He and Leclerc have each won a race this year.

Ferrari started the season with the best chassis in terms of cornering performance, but their engine has fallen short of those produced by Mercedes and Red Bull.

Hamilton said: "We're second in the championship, a huge improvement on last year already. And that's with a deficit on power of average 0.4secs [per lap] every single weekend. Some races it's 0.6sec and we've still be delivering really great performances.

"And that just highlights how great a job people at the factory have done. All the negativity takes away from that.

"Of course we're not where we want to be but you don't go from last year's experience straight to number one. It's a process and I think we've built a good foundation this year, we need to continue to build on it. We're not perfect yet but I do believe we can get there.

I think we've had the best car this year. But it's unfortunate we have been down 0.4secs on power. That is difficult overcome but it's something we're working on for next year."

SportsTab.title: Super League Grand Final: Will 2026 finally be the year Warrington Wolves win at Old Trafford?
SportsTab.text:
Britain did not have a single motorway in 1955.

We were still five years out from the MOT being introduced and cars did not require a seatbelt.

There was one television channel, provided by the BBC.

Capital punishment was still in place.

The humble postcode had not yet been rolled out across the land.

And rationing was still very much in the national memory, having only been phased out a year beforehand.

All of this paints a picture as to what life was like when Warrington last won a league championship.

On Saturday they stand 80 minutes away from ending a 71-year wait for another title and their boss Sam Burgess has the chance to lay down a marker as a coach just as he did during an illustrious playing career.

But can Super League's perennial nearly side finally get over the line and finally earn a league triumph in the modern era?

Former England captain Burgess began his career as Warrington head coach in earnest ahead of the 2024 season - off the back of Daryl Powell's uncompetitive stint in charge of the Wire.

A legend of the game as a player, it was his first top job as a coach, five years after he retired following his enviable stint both on the pitch and as assistant coach down under with South Sydney Rabbitohs.

A first Wembley appearance came shortly after, as Wolves reached that season's Challenge Cup final, when they were undone by a Wigan Warriors side on the way to a quadruple.

Twelve months later, treble-winners-in-waiting Hull KR beat them again in the final.

Burgess' side eventually missed out on a play-off spot altogether in 2025, finishing eighth, but, in contrast, they have put together a consistent campaign in 2026 to finish third in the table, behind second-placed Leeds on points difference.

So you might expect Burgess to be feeling rather pleased with himself, and his side, as they prepare for the first Grand Final of his tenure and a meeting with Powell, who has inspired Wakefield's ascent from the Championship to the top of the sport after leaving the Wire.

Well, not quite.

"Not really," Burgess replied when asked in his pre-match media commitments whether it gave him extra satisfaction that his side had proved him right by emerging as challengers after their disappointing 2025.

"I'm pretty satisfied to be here. I guess I'll find out how satisfied I am on Saturday at about eight o'clock."

It took 14 years into the Super League era before Warrington reached their first Grand Final and this year is the fifth time they have reached Old Trafford, following previous finals in 2012, 2013, 2016 and 2018.

Tony Smith's impressive Wire side came undone against Leeds first and then again at the hands of Wigan in 2013 and 2016 - with Steve Price last leading the club to a Grand Final in 2018 when they were defeated by the Warriors for a third time in a row.

Since that point, the Primrose and Blue have failed to trouble the upper echelons of the sport, with St Helens' dominant spell starting the following year while Wigan and Hull KR have both taken turns at having a commanding stint of their own.

So far this year, they have narrowly missed out on second place in the regular season and dispatched reigning champions Hull KR and Leeds in the play-offs.

Yet when times were tough in 2025, Burgess never gave up and said that it was a belief in his side and the knowledge that Warrington had a long-term plan that kept his camp motivated.

"I could see a lot of green shoots last year where we're going," he added.

"You've got to be able to believe it to do it, and I believed in the club, I believed in the players we had, and I believed in the philosophy that we've got, so I guess we've been very consistent all year without jumping out at anyone, which is a good sign.

"We've had a lot of challenges throughout the year, we've managed them well as a club, which has been important."

Ask those in the know at the beginning of the 2026 season which two teams would contest the Grand Final and not many would have picked out Warrington or Wakefield.

"It's Warrington's year" has become something of a meme in the northern hemisphere's rugby league fandom in the past few years - describing how one of the league's best-funded and well-supported teams always looks the part, but falls at the final hurdle.

Former England coach Steve McNamara arrived at the club as an assistant coach last October following his departure from a spell at Catalans, who he guided to the Challenge Cup and two Super League Grand Finals.

He is set to join Hull FC for next season but Burgess believes their previous failures have not happened in a vacuum - but have shaped the team they have become this season.

"We've played a couple of big games over the last three years, so we've got a bit of experience," said Burgess.

"We have matured as a group and as a club. The club has matured with us, which is important. Whether it counts as much, on Saturday, we'll see."

Of course, Burgess' time as a player can be summed up by a stunning 2014 season which culminated in a victorious NRL Grand Final with the Rabbitohs, when he played on with a broken cheekbone and also won the Clive Churchill Medal as man of the match.

Asked about how he reflected on that moment ahead of his first Grand Final as a coach, Burgess said: "It's much easier as a player.

"Any experience is experience whether it's as a player, coach, staff member, assistant, whatever. We've got a bit of experience in the room.

"Steve McNamara brought a lot of experience to us this year as well, which is going to help for something.

"We've got a lot of things in our corner. Again, when the whistle blows at six o'clock, you've got to do the right jobs and get the performance on the field."
